From one corner you can draw lines to every other corner and split the polygon into n − 2 triangles; each triangle has 180°. Hexagon: 4 triangles → 4 × 180° = 720°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon always add to 360°, so each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360°/n, and interior + exterior = 180° at every corner. Quick checks: each interior angle 150° → exterior 30° → n = 360/30 = 12 (dodecagon) · a polygon with 9 diagonals → n(n − 3)/2 = 9 → n = 6 (hexagon) · interior sum 1440° → n − 2 = 8 → n = 10 (decagon).

0, 1, 5, 6 fixed; 4, 9 every 2 3⁹⁹⁹·7¹⁰⁰⁰ → 7 × 1 = 7 Percent, profit, average Idea Rule Example % change (new − old)/old × 100 old 40 → new 50: +25 % Successive changes (1 + a)(1 + b) − 1 = a + b + ab +10 % then −10 % → −1 % Profit / loss profit % = (SP − CP)/CP × 100 CP 1700, SP 1800 → 5 15/17 % Discount, tax SP = MP(1 − d); price with tax = SP(1 + t) work back by dividing: 3186/1.18/1.20 = Weighted average Σwᵢxᵢ / Σwᵢ boys 4/7, girls 3/7 of candidates Ratio x : y = a : b → x = ak, y = bk — Speed, time & work Idea Rule Example Distance d = v·t; km/h × 5/18 = m/s 45 km/h = 12.5 m/s Relative speed same direction v₁ − v₂, opposite v₁ + v₂ — Train crossing train length (+ platform/bridge length) = v·t 12.5 × 30 − 130 = 245 m Boats & streams down = u + v, up = u − v → u = (down + up)/2, v = (down − up)/2 up 2, down 6 → still water 4 km/h Work & pipes rates add: 1/T = 1/T₁ + 1/T₂; emptying pipe subtracts 2 h and 4 h together → 4/3 h = 80 min Clock & calendar angle |30H − 5.5M|; hands meet every 65 5/11 min; leap year = 2 odd days — Sets & Venn diagrams Idea Rule Example Two sets n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B); CALCULUS BY PICTURE DERIVATIVE CIRCLE · INTEGRAL = AREA UNDER THE GRAPH Derivative = next function clockwise sin x d/dx sin x = cos x d/dx cos x = −sin x d/dx tan x = sec²x d/dx d/dx cot x = −cosec²x −cos x cos x clockwise d/dx sec x = sec x tan x ∫ dx: anticlockwise d/dx cosec x = −cosec x cot x Rule: every co- function (cos, cot, cosec) gets a MINUS sign in its derivative. −sin x tan ↔ sec², cot ↔ cosec², sec → sec·tan, cosec → cosec·cot ∫ −1 3 4 dx ∫ −3 3 |x| dx ∫ 0 1 √(1 − x²) dx 4 × 4 4.5 4.5 ¼ circle rectangle = 4 × 4 = 16 2 triangles = 4.5 + 4.5 = 9 quarter circle = π/4 ≈ 0.785 ∫ 0 π sin x dx ∫ 0 2 x dx ∫ −π π sin x dx +2 −2 ½·2·2 one hump = 2 triangle = ½ × 2 × 2 = 2 odd function: +2 − 2 = 0 Area trick: when the graph is a rectangle, triangle or part of a circle, the definite integral is just that area. Area below the x-axis counts as negative, so odd functions over −a to a give 0.

CALCULUS BY PICTURE (2) MAXIMA & MINIMA · ROLLE · MEAN VALUE · CONVEX · TWO-VARIABLE TEST 1 · Maxima and minima (one variable) 2 · Rolle's theorem max: f′ = 0, f″ < 0 f′(c) = 0 min: f′ = 0, f″ > 0 x a b x Slope f′ = 0 at a turning point. Bending down (f″ < 0) → f continuous on [a, b], differentiable inside, and f(a) = f(b) → maximum; bending up (f″ > 0) → minimum. On a closed somewhere between, the tangent is flat: f′(c) = 0. interval also check the end points. 3 · Lagrange mean value theorem 4 · Convex function chord chord above curve tangent at c ∥ chord only minimum x x Somewhere between a and b the tangent is parallel to the f″ > 0 everywhere → convex: every chord lies above the chord: f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a). For f = x²/4 on [0.5, 3.5]: c curve, at most one minimum and no interior maximum (e x is = 2 (the midpoint for any parabola). convex but has no minimum). Two-variable maxima / minima (13 GATE questions) Two variables f(x, y): solve f x = 0 and f y = 0 → stationary points. Then r = f xx , s = f xy , t = f yy . rt − s² > 0 and r < 0 → maximum · rt − s² > 0 and r > 0 → minimum · rt − s² < 0 → saddle point (up one way, down the other) · rt − s² = 0 → test fails, look further. Example: f = x² + y² − 4x → f x = 2x − 4 = 0, f y = 2y = 0 → (2, 0); r = 2, s = 0, t = 2 → rt − s² = 4 > 0, r > 0 → minimum f = −4.

p: EEE Magic Numbers Each card gives the number, its exact form, every formula it sits in (with the topic), a one-line way to remember it and a quick check. Formula in doubt? Values where it doesn't matter 13 If every value is 2 (or 1, 0, 45°), plus and multiply give the same answer Used for: the exam moment when you cannot recall whether a formula adds or multiplies, squares or doubles, or which way up a ratio goes. Identity What it means for you 2 + 2 = 2 × 2 = 2² = 4 With 2, add / multiply / square all give 4 — if every number in the sum is 2, either form gives the same answer x² = 2x only at x = 2 Confused between x² and 2x? At x = 2 both are 4 — answer is safe; for any other value you must know which x + x = 2x ; x · x = x² Same value added → ×2; same value multiplied → square 1ⁿ = 1 ; 1 × a = a ; √1 = 1 With 1, powers and roots vanish — a formula error in the exponent cannot change the answer 0 × anything = 0 ; e⁰ = 1 ; ln 1 = 0 Zero / one values kill terms — check what remains a/b = b/a only when a = b Ratio upside-down? If the two values are equal the answer is 1 either way R ∥ R = R/2 ; R + R = 2R Equal resistors: series doubles, parallel halves cos 45° = sin 45° = 0.707 ; tan 45° = 1 At 45° sin and cos are interchangeable; R = X gives 45° √2 × √2 = 2 ; √3 × √3 = 3 RMS × √2 and line ÷ √3 cancel neatly ★ If the given numbers make both forms equal (all values 2, equal R's, 45°, 1 or 0), choose either — the answer is the same. But never use 2 to TEST a formula you are unsure of: it hides the mistake. Test with 3 instead (3 + 3 = 6 but 3 × 3 = 9).

Formula in doubt? 9 quick tests that settle it 14 Units, extremes, equal values, limits, symmetry Used for: deciding between two half-remembered formulas in under 30 seconds, and catching an upside-down ratio before you mark the option. Test How to apply Example Units / dimensions Both sides must have the same unit. P = V²/R gives W ✓; P = V/R² gives A/Ω ✗ √(L/C) is Ω ✓ ; √(LC) is s ✓ (time) — so 1/√(LC) is rad/s Extreme value: put 0 R = 0 or X = 0 — does the answer make physical sense? Series R‖C at R = 0 must give pure capacitor Extreme value: put ∞ Open circuit / very large value R L → ∞ in a divider → output = full source voltage Equal values Two equal items must share equally Parallel generators of equal X share load 50 : 50 Known special case Formula must reduce to the textbook case Three-phase P = √3 V L I L cos φ must equal 3 V ph I ph cos φ (star: V L = √3 V ph ) Bigger / smaller check Does increasing an input push the answer the right way? More load → more Cu loss; higher X → lower P max Limits 0 ≤ answer ≤ 1 pf, efficiency, slip (motor), probability, ζ for underdamped η = 1.2 or pf = 1.5 means the formula is upside-down Symmetry Swapping two identical items must not change the result Z₁ ∥ Z₂ formula is symmetric in Z₁, Z₂ ✓ Check with 3, not 2 3 separates the forms: 3 + 3 = 6, but 3 × 3 = 3² = 9 (with 2 all give 4) Pick 3 (or 10) when testing which form is right ★ Fastest order: units → put 0 or ∞ → equal values. One of the three usually kills the wrong option.

Engineering Mathematics 1 Matrices — eigenvalues of a 2×2 matrix KEY FORMULA λ² − (trace)λ + det = 0 What it means The eigenvalues of a 2×2 matrix are the two roots of this quadratic. You only need the trace (a + d) and the determinant (ad − bc). Letters & units λ = eigenvalue; trace = sum of diagonal elements; det = |A| When to use Any 'find the eigenvalues' question. For bigger matrices use: sum of eigenvalues = trace, product = determinant. Worked example A = [4 1; 2 3]: trace 7, det 10 → λ² − 7λ + 10 = 0 → λ = 5, 2. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Matrix Trace Det Eigenvalues [2 0; 0 3] 5 6 2, 3 (diagonal) [1 2; 2 1] 2 −3 3, −1 [4 1; 2 3] 7 10 5, 2 [2 1; 1 2] 4 3 3, 1 [3 1; 0 5] 8 15 3, 5 (triangular) [1 1; 1 1] 2 0 2, 0 [0 1; −1 0] 0 1 ±i [1 1 1; 1 1 1; 1 1 1] 3 0 3, 0, 0 (TNEB 2018) Also remember: A⁻¹ has 1/λ; A² has λ²; kA has kλ; A + kI has λ + k. REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away Eigenvalues 2 and 3 → trace 5, det 6 One eigenvalue 0 → det = 0 (singular) ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table α V d / V d0 V LL = 100 kV V LL = 200 kV 0° 1 135.1 kV 270.1 kV 15° 0.966 130.4 kV 260.9 kV 30° 0.866 117 kV 233.9 kV 45° 0.707 95.5 kV 191 kV 60° 0.5 67.5 kV 135.1 kV 90° 0 0 kV 0 kV 150° -0.866 -117 kV -233.9 kV ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. V LL = 200 kV, α = 0: V d0 ? 270 kV 2. α for zero V d ? 90° ⚠ Common MCQ trap: 1.35 multiplies the RMS LINE voltage (3√2/π).

45 Series compensation — power transfer KEY FORMULA P max = V s V r / [X L (1 − k)] What it means A series capacitor cancels part of the line reactance, so more power can be transferred. Letters & units k = degree of compensation = X C /X L When to use Loadability with series capacitors. Worked example k = 0.5 → P max doubles. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table k Effective X P max increase 0.2 0.8 X L 1.25× 0.25 0.75 X L 1.33× 0.4 0.6 X L 1.67× 0.5 0.5 X L 2× 0.6 0.4 X L 2.5× 0.7 0.3 X L 3.33× REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away P max doubled → k = 0.5 P max × 1.33 → k = 0.25 ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. 40% compensation: P max ? ×1.67 2. X L = 100 Ω, X C = 30 Ω: k? 0.3 ⚠ Common MCQ trap: P max rises by 1/(1 − k), not (1 + k).

46 Energy meter and CT KEY FORMULA Revolutions = kWh × meter constant; I secondary = I primary × (5/CT primary) What it means The meter constant tells revolutions per kWh. A CT scales the line current down to 5 A (or 1 A) for meters and relays. Letters & units Meter constant in rev/kWh; CT ratio e.g. 400/5 When to use Meter testing, error, CT secondary current questions. Worked example 1 kW for 1 hour on a 600 rev/kWh meter → 600 revolutions. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Primary current CT 100/5 CT 400/5 CT 1000/5 50 A 2.5 A 0.625 A 0.25 A 100 A 5 A 1.25 A 0.5 A 400 A 20 A 5 A 2 A 1000 A 50 A 12.5 A 5 A 4000 A 200 A 50 A 20 A Also remember: Meter error % = (recorded − true)/true × 100. Never open a CT secondary on load. ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. 2 kW for 30 min, 1200 rev/kWh? 1200 rev 2. CT 200/5, line 160 A: secondary? 4 A ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Relay/meter sees CT SECONDARY current.

47 PV energy yield and fill factor KEY FORMULA E (kWh/day) = kWp × peak sun hours × PR; FF = V mp I mp /(V oc I sc ) What it means Daily energy depends on the installed peak power, the equivalent full-sun hours and the system losses (performance ratio). Letters & units kWp = rated DC power; PR ≈ 0.75–0.8 When to use Rooftop solar sizing, energy per year. Worked example 3 kWp × 4.5 h × 0.8 = 10.8 kWh/day ≈ 3,942 kWh/year. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Plant kWh/day (4.5 h, PR 0.8) kWh/year 1 kWp 3.6 1,314 3 kWp 10.8 3,942 5 kWp 18 6,570 10 kWp 36 13,140 100 kWp 131,400 1000 kWp 3,600 1,314,000 Also remember: Fill factor 0.7–0.8; mono-Si efficiency ≈ 20%; about 6–7 m² of panel per kWp. ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. 5 kWp, 5 sun-hours, PR 0.8? 20 kWh/day 2. V oc 40, I sc 9, P max 270 W: FF? 0.75 ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Use peak SUN HOURS, not daylight hours.

48 Wind turbine — power vs rotor size KEY FORMULA P = ½ ρ π R² v³ C p What it means Power grows with the square of blade length and the cube of wind speed. Letters & units R = blade radius (m); v = wind speed; C p ≈ 0.4 practical When to use Turbine output questions. Worked example R = 40 m, v = 10 m/s, C p = 0.4 → P ≈ 1.23 MW. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Blade radius v = 6 m/s v = 8 m/s v = 10 m/s v = 12 m/s 10 m 17 kW 39 kW 77 kW 133 kW 20 m 67 kW 158 kW 308 kW 532 kW 30 m 150 kW 355 kW 693 kW 1,197 kW 40 m 266 kW 631 kW 1,232 kW 2,128 kW 50 m 416 kW 985 kW 1,924 kW 3,325 kW REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away Power × 8 → wind speed × 2 Power × 4 → blade length × 2 ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. R = 20 m, v = 10 m/s, C p 0.4? 308 kW 2. Speed 8 → 12 m/s: power? ×3.375 ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Area uses R² — double blade length → 4× power.

49 Autotransformer — kVA from a two-winding transformer KEY FORMULA S auto = S 2w × V out /V series ; transformed = S 2w , conducted = S auto − S 2w ; Cu saved = k = V L /V H What it means Reconnect the two windings in series: the full rated current of the series winding now flows at the higher output voltage, so the same windings carry a much larger kVA. Only S 2w is transformed; the rest is conducted straight through. Letters & units S 2w = two-winding rating; V series = voltage of the winding put in series; V out = output (high) voltage; k = V L /V H of the autotransformer When to use 'A two-winding transformer is reconnected as an autotransformer — find the new kVA', copper saving and efficiency questions. Worked example 50 kVA, 2400/240 V with the 240 V winding in series → 2640/2400 V: S = 50 × 2640/240 = 550 kVA (11×). Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Two-winding Winding in series Autotransformer kVA Cu saved (k) 50 kVA, 2400/240 V 240 V 2640/2400 V 90.9 % 10 kVA, 220/110 V 110 V 330/220 V 30 66.7 % 10 kVA, 220/110 V 220 V 330/110 V 15 33.3 % 100 kVA, 11000/2200 V 2200 V 13200/11000 V 83.3 % 5 kVA, 400/100 V 100 V 500/400 V 25 80 % 20 kVA, 230/115 V 115 V 345/230 V 60 66.7 % Also remember: Losses stay those of the two-winding transformer while the output rises, so η auto is higher. Disadvantage: no electrical isolation between the windings. REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away 50 kVA, 2400/240 V → 2640/2400 V auto → 550 kVA 10 kVA, 220/110 V → 330/220 V → 30 kVA ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. 20 kVA, 230/115 V → 345/230 V auto: rating? 60 kVA 2. Cu saved for 345/230 V auto? k = 230/345 = 66.7 % ⚠ Common MCQ trap: The winding put in SERIES decides the rating: S auto = S 2w × V out /V series — not S 2w × turns ratio.

50 Two-wattmeter method — pf from the reading ratio KEY FORMULA P = W₁ + W₂, Q = √3 (W₁ − W₂), tan φ = √3 (W₁ − W₂)/(W₁ + W₂) What it means With a balanced load W₁ = V L I L cos(30° − φ) and W₂ = V L I L cos(30° + φ). Their ratio alone fixes the power-factor angle. Letters & units W₁ = larger reading; W₂ = smaller reading (negative if reversed); φ = load (impedance) angle When to use 'One wattmeter reads twice the other', 'one reads zero', 'one reads negative' — find pf or φ. Worked example W₁ = 2W₂: tan φ = √3 (1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5) = 0.577 → φ = 30°, pf = 0.866. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table W₂/W₁ tan φ φ pf 1 0 0° 1 0.75 0.247 13.9° 0.971 0.5 0.577 30° 0.866 0.25 1.039 46.1° 0.693 0 1.732 60° 0.5 −0.25 2.887 70.9° 0.327 −0.5 5.196 79.1° 0.189 −1 ∞ 90° 0 Also remember: Equal readings → pf 1; one reading zero → pf 0.5 (φ = 60°); one negative → pf < 0.5 (reverse its current coil and subtract); equal and opposite → pf 0. REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away W₁ = 2W₂ → pf 0.866 W₂ = 0 → pf 0.5 W₁ = W₂ → pf 1 ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. W₁ = 8 kW, W₂ = 4 kW: pf? tan φ = 0.577 → 0.866 2. W₁ = 5 kW, W₂ = −1 kW: P? 4 kW ⚠ Common MCQ trap: A negative reading is subtracted (P = W₁ − |W₂|); tan φ uses the signed values.

Electronics, Communication & Processors 51 Rectifiers — output values KEY FORMULA Half-wave V dc = V m /π; full-wave V dc = 2V m /π What it means A full-wave rectifier uses both half cycles, so it gives twice the DC output and much less ripple. Letters & units V m = peak secondary voltage When to use Rectifier DC output, ripple and PIV questions. Worked example V m = 100 V → half-wave 31.8 V, full-wave 63.7 V. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Parameter Half-wave Full-wave (CT) Bridge V dc 0.318 V m 0.637 V m 0.637 V m V rms 0.5 V m 0.707 V m 0.707 V m Ripple factor 1.21 0.482 0.482 Efficiency 40.6% 81.2% 81.2% PIV V m 2V m V m TUF 0.287 0.693 0.812 Ripple frequency 50 Hz 100 Hz 100 Hz REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away V dc = 63.7 V, full-wave → V m = 100 V Ripple 0.482 → full-wave TUF 0.287 → half-wave ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. Bridge, V m = 50 V: V dc ? 31.8 V 2. Half-wave V dc = 10 V: V m ? 31.4 V ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Bridge PIV = V m ; centre-tap PIV = 2V m . See: Complete Formula Book → Analog Electronics — Diodes & Rectifiers · TNEB AE 2018 paper → —

52 BJT — α and β KEY FORMULA β = α/(1 − α), α = β/(1 + β) What it means α is the fraction of emitter current reaching the collector; β is collector current per unit base current. Letters & units α = I C /I E (< 1); β = I C /I B When to use Transistor current-gain conversions. Worked example α = 0.98 → β = 49. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table α β 0.9 9 0.95 19 0.96 24 0.98 49 0.99 99 0.995 Also remember: V T = 26 mV at 300 K; g m = I C /V T → 1 mA gives 38.5 mS; r e = 26 mV/I E → 26 Ω at 1 mA. REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away β = 99 → α = 0.99 β = 49 → α = 0.98 β = 19 → α = 0.95 ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. I B = 20 µA, β = 100: I C ? 2 mA 2. I C = 1 mA: g m ? 38.5 mS ⚠ Common MCQ trap: α < 1 always; β is large (50–300).

53 Op-amp gain KEY FORMULA Inverting A = −R f /R₁; non-inverting A = 1 + R f /R₁ What it means With an ideal op-amp both inputs sit at the same voltage (virtual short), so the gain depends only on the resistors. Letters & units R f = feedback resistor; R₁ = input resistor When to use Amplifier gain questions. Worked example R f = 10 kΩ, R₁ = 1 kΩ → inverting −10, non-inverting 11. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table R f / R₁ Inverting Non-inverting Gain in dB (non-inv.) 1 -1 2 6 2 -2 3 9.5 4 -4 5 14 9 -9 10 20 10 -10 11 20.8 99 -99 40 -100 40.1 REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away Non-inverting gain 11 → R f /R₁ = 10 Inverting gain −5 → R f /R₁ = 5 ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. R₁ = 2 kΩ, R f = 20 kΩ inverting, V in = 0.5 V? −5 V 2. Voltage follower gain? 1 ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Non-inverting gain is 1 + R f /R₁, not R f /R₁.

54 555 timer KEY FORMULA Astable f = 1.44/[(R A + 2R B )C]; monostable T = 1.1RC What it means Capacitor charges between ⅓ and ⅔ of V CC ; the resistor–capacitor values set the timing. Letters & units R in Ω, C in F When to use Frequency, pulse width, duty cycle questions. Worked example R A = R B = 10 kΩ, C = 0.1 µF → f = 1.44/(30k × 0.1µ) = 480 Hz. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table R A R B C Frequency Duty cycle 1 kΩ 1 kΩ 1 µF 480 Hz 66.7% 10 kΩ 10 kΩ 0.1 µF 480 Hz 66.7% 1 kΩ 10 kΩ 0.01 µF 6,857.1 Hz 52.4% 4.7 kΩ 4.7 kΩ 1 µF 102.1 Hz 66.7% 10 kΩ 100 kΩ 1 µF 6.9 Hz 52.4% REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away Duty ≈ 50% → R B ≫ R A T = 1.1 ms monostable, C = 1 µF → R = 1 kΩ ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. Monostable R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 µF: T? 110 ms 2. Astable R A = R B = 1 kΩ, C = 1 µF: f? 480 Hz ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Astable uses R A + 2R B , not R A + R B .

55 Digital — powers of 2 KEY FORMULA Number of combinations = 2ⁿ What it means n binary digits give 2ⁿ distinct values: address lines → memory locations, bits → ADC levels, flip-flops → counter states. Letters & units n = bits / address lines / flip-flops When to use Memory size, counters, ADC resolution, MUX select lines. Worked example 16 address lines → 2¹⁶ = 65,536 = 64 KB (8085). Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Memory with n address ADC step for 10 V full n 2ⁿ lines scale 4 16 16 B 625 mV 8 256 B 39.062 mV 10 1,024 1 KB 9.766 mV 12 4,096 4 KB 2.441 mV 16 65,536 64 KB 0.153 mV 20 1,048,576 1 MB 0.01 mV Also remember: Mod-N counter needs n flip-flops with 2ⁿ ≥ N. Ring: n states; Johnson: 2n states. REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away 64 KB memory → 16 address lines 1 MB → 20 lines 1024 levels → 10 bits ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. Address lines for 32 KB? 15 2. Levels of a 12-bit ADC? ⚠ Common MCQ trap: 1 KB = 1024 bytes, not 1000. See: Complete Formula Book → Digital Electronics · TNEB AE 2018 paper → Q92, Q96

56 8086 physical address KEY FORMULA Physical address = segment × 10H + offset What it means The 16-bit segment is shifted left by one hex digit (× 16) and added to the 16-bit offset to form a 20-bit address. Letters & units Segment = CS, DS, SS or ES; offset = IP, SI, DI, BX, SP … When to use Address calculation in 8086 questions. Worked example CS = 2000H, IP = 0100H → 20100H. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Segment Offset Physical address 1000H 0020H 10020H 2000H 0100H 20100H 3000H FFFFH 3FFFFH 1234H 0022H 12362H FFFFH 000FH FFFFFH (top of 1 MB) ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. DS = 4000H, offset 0005H? 40005H 2. Max memory of 8086? 1 MB ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Shift the SEGMENT left (×16), not the offset. See: Complete Formula Book → Code 400 Supplement: 8086 · TNEB AE 2018 paper → —

57 Power converters — output voltage multipliers KEY FORMULA 1-φ full: V dc = (2V m /π) cos α; 3-φ full: V dc = 1.35 V L cos α What it means The average output falls as cos α. Beyond 90° the average goes negative (inverter mode). Letters & units α = firing angle; V m = peak; V L = RMS line voltage When to use Controlled rectifier output, pf and inversion questions. Worked example 3-φ, 415 V, α = 60° → 1.35 × 415 × 0.5 = 280 V. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table α cos α 1-φ full (230 V) 3-φ full (415 V) 0° 1 207 V 560.2 V 30° 0.866 179.3 V 485.2 V 45° 0.707 146.4 V 396.2 V 60° 0.5 103.5 V 280.1 V 90° 0 0 V 0 V 120° -0.5 -103.5 V -280.1 V 150° -0.866 -179.3 V -485.2 V Also remember: Buck V o = D·V s ; boost V o = V s /(1 − D): D = 0.5 → 2V s , D = 0.75 → 4V s . REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away V dc = 0 → α = 90° V dc negative → α > 90° (inverter) V dc = ½ max → α = 60° ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. 1-φ full, 230 V, α = 60°? 103.5 V 2. 3-φ full, 400 V, α = 0? 540 V ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Semi-converter uses (1 + cos α)/π, not cos α. See: Complete Formula Book → Power Electronics · TNEB AE 2018 paper → Q86, Q89

58 Sampling and FFT KEY FORMULA f s ≥ 2f m ; FFT multiplications = (N/2) log₂N What it means Sample at least twice the highest frequency to avoid aliasing. The FFT reduces DFT work from N² to (N/2)log₂N. Letters & units f m = highest signal frequency; N = number of points When to use Nyquist rate, DFT/FFT computation questions. Worked example Voice 3.4 kHz → Nyquist 6.8 kHz (telephone uses 8 kHz). Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table N DFT (N²) FFT ((N/2)log₂N) Saving 8 64 12 5.3× 16 32 8× 64 4,096 21.3× 65,536 1,024 64× 1,048,576 5,120 204.8× REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away f s = 8 kHz → max f m = 4 kHz 10 stages FFT → N = 1024 ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. Signal 20 kHz max: Nyquist rate? 40 kHz 2. FFT of 512 points: stages? 9 ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Nyquist rate is 2f m (not f m ). See: Complete Formula Book → Signals, Systems & DSP · TNEB AE 2018 paper → Q102, Q105

59 AM — power and efficiency KEY FORMULA P t = P c (1 + m²/2), η = m²/(2 + m²) What it means The carrier carries no information; sidebands carry m²/2 of the carrier power, so efficiency is low for AM. Letters & units m = modulation index; P c = carrier power When to use Transmitted power, efficiency, current questions. Worked example m = 1 → P t = 1.5 P c , η = 33.3%. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table m P t / P c I t / I c Efficiency 0.25 1.031 1.016 3% 0.3 1.045 1.022 4.3% 0.5 1.125 1.061 11.1% 0.6 1.18 1.086 15.3% 0.8 1.32 1.149 24.2% 1 1.5 1.225 33.3% REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away P t = 1.5 P c → m = 1 η = 24% → m ≈ 0.8 P t = 1.125 P c → m = 0.5 ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. P c = 10 kW, m = 0.6: P t ? 11.8 kW 2. m = 0.5: η? 11.1% ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Efficiency uses m², not m. See: Complete Formula Book → Communication Engineering · TNEB AE 2018 paper → Q113, Q117

60 PCM — levels and SQNR KEY FORMULA L = 2ⁿ, SQNR ≈ 1.76 + 6.02 n dB What it means Each extra bit doubles the number of levels and improves signal-to-quantisation-noise by about 6 dB. Letters & units n = bits per sample; L = quantisation levels When to use PCM bandwidth, levels and noise questions. Worked example 8-bit PCM: 256 levels, ≈ 50 dB. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Bit rate at 8 kHz Bits n Levels SQNR (dB) sampling 4 16 25.8 32 kbps 6 64 37.9 48 kbps 7 43.9 56 kbps 8 49.9 64 kbps 10 1,024 62 80 kbps 12 4,096 74 96 kbps 16 65,536 98.1 128 kbps Also remember: PCM bandwidth (minimum) = n·f s /2. Entropy of M equally likely messages = log₂M bits. REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away 256 levels → 8 bits SQNR ≈ 50 dB → 8 bits +12 dB wanted → 2 more bits ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. 7 bits, f s 8 kHz: bit rate? 56 kbps 2. Levels for 5 bits? 32 ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Levels = 2ⁿ, not 2n. See: Complete Formula Book → Communication Engineering · TNEB AE 2018 paper → Q114, Q118

61 Chopper — output vs duty cycle KEY FORMULA Buck V o = D V s ; Boost V o = V s /(1 − D); Buck-boost V o = −D V s /(1 − D) What it means Duty cycle D = T on /T sets the output. Buck lowers, boost raises, buck-boost can do both (inverted). Letters & units D = duty cycle (0 to 1); V s = input voltage When to use DC-DC converter questions. Worked example V s = 100 V, D = 0.75 → buck 75 V, boost 400 V, buck-boost −300 V. Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table D Buck Boost Buck-boost 0.2 20 V 125 V -25 V 0.25 25 V 133.3 V -33.3 V 0.4 40 V 166.7 V -66.7 V 0.5 50 V 200 V -100 V 0.6 60 V 250 V -150 V 0.75 75 V 400 V -300 V 0.8 80 V 500 V -400 V Also remember: Values for V s = 100 V — scale proportionally. REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away Boost gives 2V s → D = 0.5 Buck gives 0.25V s → D = 0.25 Buck-boost |V o | = V s → D = 0.5 ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. Buck, 48 V, D = 0.25? 12 V 2. Boost, 12 V → 48 V: D? 0.75 ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Boost is V s /(1 − D), not V s /D. See: Complete Formula Book → Power Electronics · TNEB AE 2018 paper → Q87

62 Counters and flip-flops KEY FORMULA Flip-flops needed n = ⌈log₂ N⌉ What it means A mod-N counter needs enough flip-flops that 2ⁿ ≥ N; unused states are skipped with feedback. Letters & units N = modulus; n = flip-flops When to use Counter design and frequency division. Worked example Mod-10 (decade) counter → 4 flip-flops (2⁴ = 16 ≥ 10). Direct Answers — read the answer straight from the table Modulus N Flip-flops Output frequency (1 MHz clock) 2 1 500 kHz 3 2 333.33 kHz 5 3 200 kHz 6 3 166.67 kHz 8 3 125 kHz 10 4 100 kHz 12 4 83.33 kHz 16 4 62.5 kHz 60 6 16.67 kHz Also remember: Ring counter: n flip-flops → n states. Johnson counter: n flip-flops → 2n states. REVERSE LOOKUP — given the answer-side value, find the input If the question gives… …answer straight away 4 flip-flops → mod up to 16 Divide by 60 → 6 flip-flops ONE-MINUTE NUMERICALS — cover the right column, solve, then check 1. Mod-12 counter flip-flops? 4 2. Johnson counter, 4 FF: states? 8 ⚠ Common MCQ trap: Mod-N needs ⌈log₂N⌉ flip-flops, not N. See: Complete Formula Book → Digital Electronics · TNEB AE 2018 paper → Q92

g.d: 42 grids that compare a whole family at once: machines, relays, power plants, converters, logic families, ADCs, numerical methods …
p: TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — Cross-Comparison Book ⇄ Cross-Comparison Book 42 grids: machines, measurements, power, electronics, control + formula toolkit Exam options are often neighbours: shunt or series, Hay or Maxwell, mho or reactance, SF₆ or vacuum. If you learn each topic alone, they blur. Here every family is in one grid with the same rows, so the difference jumps out when you read across a row. How to use it ① Read Part 1 row by row (not column by column). ② Learn the ★ memory hook. ③ Answer the 2 exam traps. ④ Next day, fill the blank grid in Part 2 from memory, then check with Part 1. p: TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places ∞ One Concept, Many Places 28 formula families that repeat across all electrical subjects Electrical engineering keeps reusing the same few ideas. A transformer, an induction motor and a CT all use the same EMF equation; a synchronous machine and a transmission line use the same power–angle curve; a transformer and a DC machine reach maximum efficiency by the same rule. Learn each idea once here, then see where it reappears. TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 1 Faraday's EMF equation Appears in: Transformer, CT / PT, DC machine, Induction motor, Synchronous machine, Power electronics Every machine that has a coil and a changing flux makes voltage the same way. Only the name of the machine changes. e = N·dΦ/dt → for sine flux: E(rms) = 4.44 · f · N · Φm Where Same idea written there Remember Transformer E₁ = 4.44 f N₁ Φm , E₂ = 4.44 f N₂ Φm → E₁/E₂ = N₁/N₂ Φm ∝ V/f. Same V, lower f → core saturates. Alternator (synchronous gen.) Eph = 4.44 f Φ Tph Kw (Kw = Kp·Kd), f = PN/120 Same equation + winding factor (short pitch, distribution). Induction motor E₁ = 4.44 f N₁ Φ Kw₁ ; rotor running: E₂s = s·E₂ , f₂ = s·f IM = 'rotating transformer' with secondary frequency s·f.
