Synchronous machine Zs = Ra + jXs Xs = Xleakage + Xarmature-reaction. Transformer Zeq = Req + jXeq (referred) X/R ratio decides fault offset. Induction motor Rotor reactance at standstill X₂, running s X₂ Low-slip: rotor nearly resistive. Transmission line Series Z = R + jωL per km; shunt Y = jωC per km ABCD from Z and Y. Harmonics h-th harmonic: XL × h , XC ÷ h Capacitor banks overload on harmonics. ★ Memory hook: f up → XL up, XC down. R stays the same. Quick check — exam style Q. Frequency doubled. XL and XC? → XL doubles, XC halves. Q. L = 0.1 H at 50 Hz. Reactance? → XL = 2π × 50 × 0.1 ≈ 31.4 Ω. Q. 5th-harmonic voltage on a capacitor bank. Capacitor reactance? → XC ÷ 5 → it draws 5 times more current per volt. 1794 p 1794 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 19 Feedback — one rule for amplifiers, op-amps, oscillators and control Appears in: Circuits, Electronics, Control, Faults / stability / load flow Feed part of the output back and compare it with the input. Negative feedback trades gain for everything else; positive feedback with loop gain 1 makes an oscillator. Af = A / (1 + Aβ) · closed loop C/R = G / (1 + GH) · oscillation: Aβ = 1 at 0° (Barkhausen) Where Same idea written there Remember Transistor amplifier Af = A/(1 + Aβ); bandwidth × (1 + Aβ); distortion and noise ÷ (1 + Aβ) Gain-bandwidth product stays constant. Feedback topology Series mixing raises Zin × (1 + Aβ); shunt mixing lowers it; voltage sampling lowers Zout ÷ (1 + Aβ) Voltage-series = the ideal voltage amplifier. Op-amp Huge A → Af ≈ 1/β: inverting −Rf/R₁, non-inverting 1 + Rf/R₁ The resistors, not the op-amp, set the gain. Oscillators Positive feedback, |Aβ| = 1, total phase 0° or 360° RC phase-shift needs A ≥ 29; Wien bridge A ≥ 3. Control systems C/R = G/(1 + GH); sensitivity to G ÷ (1 + GH); ess falls as loop gain rises Same (1 + loop gain) divider as the amplifier. Power systems AVR holds voltage, governor droop shares load (Δf = −R ΔP) Feedback loops on every generator. ★ Memory hook: Negative feedback: gain ÷ (1 + Aβ), bandwidth × (1 + Aβ). Positive feedback with Aβ = 1: oscillator. Quick check — exam style Q. A = 100, β = 0.04. Closed-loop gain? → Af = 100/(1 + 4) = 20. Q. Loop gain Aβ = 1 at 0° phase. Result? → Sustained oscillation (Barkhausen criterion). Q. Unity feedback, G = 10. C/R? → 10/11 ≈ 0.909. 1795 p 1795 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 20 RMS, average, form factor & peak factor Appears in: Circuits, Measurements, Power electronics, Electronics RMS is the heating value, average is what a moving-coil meter sees. Their ratio (form factor) tells you which waveform you have. Vrms = √(mean of v²) , Vavg = mean of |v| , form factor = Vrms / Vavg , peak factor = Vm / Vrms Where Same idea written there Remember Sine Vrms = Vm/√2 = 0.707 Vm; Vavg = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm; FF 1.11, PF 1.414 The numbers on every AC nameplate are rms. Square wave Vrms = Vavg = Vm; FF 1, PF 1 Flat top → rms = peak. Triangle / sawtooth Vrms = Vm/√3; Vavg = Vm/2; FF 1.155, PF 1.732 √3 for a straight-line ramp. Rectifiers Half-wave: Vdc = Vm/π, Vrms = Vm/2 (FF 1.57). Full-wave: Vdc = 2Vm/π, Vrms = Vm/√2 Ripple factor = √(FF² − 1): 1.21 half-wave, 0.48 full-wave. Measurements Moving iron and dynamometer read rms; PMMC reads average; rectifier meters are scaled by 1.11 A non-sine wave on a rectifier meter → error. Power electronics Chopper output: Vavg = D·V, Vrms = √D·V Average sets dc power; rms sets heating. DC + harmonics Vrms = √(V₀² + V₁² + V₂² + …) (each in rms) Add squares, never the values. ★ Memory hook: Heating → rms; meter needle (PMMC) → average; sine FF = 1.11. Quick check — exam style Q. Half-wave rectified sine, peak 100 V. Average and rms? → Vavg = 100/π = 31.83 V; Vrms = 50 V. Q. Square wave of ±10 V on an average-responding meter scaled for sine. Reading? → Average 10 V × 1.11 = 11.1 V (true rms is 10 V). Q. v = 10 + 10√2 sin ωt. RMS value? → √(10² + 10²) = 14.14 V. 1796 p 1796 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 21 Duty ratio & averaging Appears in: Power electronics, Electronics, Measurements, Utilisation Switch a voltage on for a fraction D of each period and the load sees the average. Every chopper, PWM drive and 555 timer works this way. Average = D·Vhigh + (1 − D)·Vlow , rms of a pulse train = V√D Where Same idea written there Remember Buck chopper V₀ = D·Vs D = 0.4 on 100 V → 40 V. Boost · buck-boost V₀ = Vs/(1 − D) · V₀ = D·Vs/(1 − D) (inverted) D → 1 makes the boost output shoot up. PWM inverter Fundamental ∝ modulation index m (linear for m ≤ 1) Average over each carrier period follows the sine. 555 astable f = 1.44/((RA + 2RB)C); D = (RA + RB)/(RA + 2RB) D is always above 50 % unless a diode bypasses RB. Integral-cycle control P = Pfull · n/(n + m); Vrms = V√(n/(n + m)) Same √D rule for the rms. Pulse train · digital clock Vavg = D·V; fundamental and harmonics set by D D = 50 % kills the even harmonics. ★ Memory hook: Average = D × V; rms = √D × V. Quick check — exam style Q. Buck chopper, Vs = 100 V, D = 0.4. Output? → 40 V. Q. Pulse train 10 V, D = 0.25. Average and rms? → Average 2.5 V; rms 10√0.25 = 5 V. Q. 555 astable, RA = 1 kΩ, RB = 2 kΩ, C = 0.1 µF. f and D? → f = 1.44/(5 kΩ × 0.1 µF) ≈ 2880 Hz; D = 3/5 = 60 %. 1797 p 1797 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 22 Decibels — one ratio scale everywhere Appears in: Electronics, Control, Communication, Measurements, Transmission line dB turns multiplication into addition. Use 10 log for power ratios and 20 log for voltage or current ratios. dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁) = 20 log₁₀(V₂/V₁) ; dBm = 10 log₁₀(P / 1 mW) ; 1 neper = 8.686 dB Where Same idea written there Remember Amplifiers Stage gains in dB simply add 20 dB + 30 dB = 50 dB (voltage × 316). Bode plots Each pole −20 dB/decade (−6 dB/octave); corner is the −3 dB point −3 dB = half power, 0.707 of the voltage. Communication SNR, path loss and noise figure in dB; power in dBm 0 dBm = 1 mW; 30 dBm = 1 W. PCM SQNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB Each extra bit adds 6 dB. Op-amps CMRR (dB) = 20 log(Ad/Ac) A CMRR of 100 dB = a ratio of 10⁵. Lines & cables Attenuation in dB/km or nepers Loss in dB adds along the route. ★ Memory hook: Power → 10 log; voltage → 20 log; ×2 power = +3 dB, ×2 voltage = +6 dB. Quick check — exam style Q. Stages of 20 dB and 30 dB in cascade. Overall voltage gain? → 50 dB = ×316. Q. 1 W in dBm? → 30 dBm. Q. Power halves. Change in dB? → −3.01 dB. 1798 p 1798 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 23 Thevenin view — any network is a source behind an impedance Appears in: Circuits, Faults / stability / load flow, Induction motor, Synchronous machine, Electronics, Measurements Seen from two terminals, a linear network is one voltage behind one impedance. Engineers use this picture in circuits, faults, machines and electronics alike. Vth = open-circuit voltage , Zth = Voc / Isc (or the impedance with sources killed) Where Same idea written there Remember Circuits Maximum power when RL = Rth: Pmax = Vth²/(4Rth) Norton: IN = Vth/Rth, same R. Fault calculation Fault current = Vprefault / Zth; Z-bus diagonal element = Zth at that bus Short-circuit MVA = base MVA / Zth (pu). Induction motor Stator side replaced by Vth, Zth → smax = R₂′/√(Rth² + (Xth + X₂′)²) Exact torque formula uses the Thevenin stator. Alternator & grid E behind Xs; the grid is an infinite bus (Zth → 0) Stiff bus = tiny Thevenin impedance. Transistor bias Divider: Vth = Vcc R₂/(R₁ + R₂), Rth = R₁ ∥ R₂ Then IB = (Vth − VBE)/(Rth + (β + 1)RE). Measurements Voltmeter loading: reading = Vth · Rv/(Rv + Rth) High-R source + low-R meter → low reading. ★ Memory hook: Open-circuit voltage + short-circuit current = the whole network. Quick check — exam style Q. Voc = 12 V, Isc = 3 A. Load for maximum power and Pmax? → Rth = 4 Ω → RL = 4 Ω, Pmax = 12²/(4 × 4) = 9 W. Q. Pre-fault 1 pu, Zth = j0.25 pu. Three-phase fault current? → 1/0.25 = 4 pu. Q. Divider R₁ = 40 kΩ, R₂ = 10 kΩ on 10 V. Vth and Rth? → Vth = 2 V; Rth = 40 ∥ 10 = 8 kΩ. 1799 p 1799 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 24 Harmonics — one Fourier idea in power, machines and electronics Appears in: Power electronics, Faults / stability / load flow, Transformer, Synchronous machine, Circuits, Measurements Any periodic non-sine wave is a fundamental plus harmonics. Odd symmetry keeps only odd harmonics; three-phase circuits trap or add the triplens. THD = √(V₂² + V₃² + …) / V₁ , Vrms = V₁√(1 + THD²) , pf = (I₁/Irms)·cos φ₁ Where Same idea written there Remember Square wave Only odd harmonics, amplitude 4V/(nπ) Fourier series of half-wave symmetry. Converters 6-pulse: 6k ± 1 (5, 7, 11, 13 …); 12-pulse: 12k ± 1 (11, 13 …) More pulses → cleaner current. Transformers Magnetising current carries a 3rd harmonic; a delta winding traps triplens Star-star needs a delta tertiary. Three-phase 4-wire Triplens are in phase in all lines → IN = 3I₃ Neutral can carry more than a line. AC machines Short pitch by 1/n of a pole pitch removes the nth harmonic (kp = cos(nα/2)) Distribution factor cuts them further. Capacitors & filters XC ÷ n at the nth harmonic → large harmonic current, resonance risk Detuned (series L) capacitor banks. Measurements Average-reading meters err on harmonics; use true-rms meters Form factor no longer 1.11. ★ Memory hook: Odd symmetry → odd harmonics; triplens add in the neutral, vanish in delta. Quick check — exam style Q. V₁ = 100, V₃ = 30, V₅ = 40 (rms). THD? → √(30² + 40²)/100 = 50 %. Q. Line-current harmonics of a 6-pulse converter? → 6k ± 1: 5, 7, 11, 13 … Q. Coil pitch that removes the 5th harmonic? → Short pitch by 1/5 of a pole pitch (kp5 = cos 90° = 0). 1800 p 1800 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 25 Sampling & aliasing Appears in: Signals & DSP, Communication, Measurements, Electronics Sample at least twice the highest frequency, or a high tone shows up disguised as a low one. fs ≥ 2 fmax (Nyquist) , a tone at f appears at |f − k·fs| , PCM bit rate = n · fs Where Same idea written there Remember DSP Anti-alias low-pass filter before the ADC; reconstruction by ideal low-pass Spectrum repeats every fs. PCM fs ≥ 2W; bit rate n·fs; bandwidth ≥ n·fs/2 Voice: 8 kHz × 8 bits = 64 kb/s. Product of signals Bandwidth of x₁·x₂ = B₁ + B₂ → Nyquist rate 2(B₁ + B₂) Squaring doubles the bandwidth. Band-pass sampling fs ≥ 2B (bandwidth), not 2fmax, under the band-position condition Used for radio IF signals. Digital instruments Sample-and-hold, then ADC; conversion must finish in 1/fs Sampling scopes rebuild fast repetitive waves. Stroboscope A rotating disc lit at fs looks still when its rate = k·fs Aliasing used on purpose to measure speed. ★ Memory hook: Twice the top frequency; alias = |f − k fs|. Quick check — exam style Q. cos(2π·300t) sampled at 400 Hz. Apparent frequency? → |300 − 400| = 100 Hz. Q. 4 kHz voice, 8 bits per sample, Nyquist sampling. Bit rate? → 8 kHz × 8 = 64 kb/s. Q. Signals of 1 kHz and 3 kHz bandwidth are multiplied. Nyquist rate? → 2 × (1 + 3) = 8 kHz. 1801 p 1801 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 26 Coupling coefficient, mutual inductance & leakage Appears in: Circuits, Transformer, Induction motor, Measurements, Communication, Transmission line Two coils share part of their flux. The shared part is mutual inductance; the part that misses is leakage. k tells how much is shared. M = k√(L₁L₂) , aiding L = L₁ + L₂ + 2M , opposing L = L₁ + L₂ − 2M , W = ½L₁I₁² + ½L₂I₂² ± M I₁I₂ Where Same idea written there Remember Coupled coils M = (Laiding − Lopposing)/4; dot convention sets the sign k ≤ 1 always. Transformer k ≈ 1 → small leakage reactance; ideal transformer k = 1 Leakage gives the series reactance X₁ + X₂′. Induction motor Air gap → larger magnetising current and more leakage than a transformer Leakage reactance limits Tmax. Measurements Mutual inductors, Campbell bridge, Rogowski coil M measured by aiding/opposing method. Communication Tuned IF transformers are loosely coupled (k < 1) to shape bandwidth Critical coupling k = 1/Q. Transmission lines Mutual coupling between parallel circuits; zero-sequence mutual is large Affects earth-fault relay reach. ★ Memory hook: Shared flux = M; missed flux = leakage; M = k√(L₁L₂). Quick check — exam style Q. L₁ = 4 mH, L₂ = 9 mH, M = 3 mH. Coupling coefficient? → k = 3/√36 = 0.5. Q. Series aiding 30 mH, opposing 14 mH. M? → (30 − 14)/4 = 4 mH. Q. Why does an induction motor draw a larger magnetising current than a transformer? → The air gap raises the reluctance. 1802 p 1802 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 27 Q factor & bandwidth Appears in: Circuits, Electronics, Communication, Measurements, Control Q compares the energy a resonant circuit stores with the energy it loses each cycle. High Q means a sharp peak and a narrow band. Q = 2π × (energy stored)/(energy lost per cycle) ; series: Q = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR) ; BW = f₀/Q Where Same idea written there Remember Series RLC Voltage magnification: VC = VL = Q·V at resonance Q = (1/R)√(L/C). Parallel RLC Current magnification: IC = IL = Q·I Q = R√(C/L). Coils Q = ωL/R measured with a Q meter Losses lower Q. Tuned amplifiers BW = f₀/Q; cascading identical stages narrows the band Selectivity of radio IF stages. Second-order systems ζ = 1/(2Q); resonant peak Mr = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)) Low damping = high Q = big peak. Filters Q = f₀/(f₂ − f₁) between the −3 dB points Same formula for band-pass filters. ★ Memory hook: Q = f₀/BW = 1/(2ζ). Quick check — exam style Q. Series R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H, C = 10 µF. f₀, Q, bandwidth? → ω₀ = 1000 rad/s (f₀ ≈ 159.2 Hz), Q = 10, BW ≈ 15.9 Hz. Q. Second-order system with ζ = 0.25. Q? → Q = 1/(2ζ) = 2. Q. Series resonance, Q = 50, source 10 V. Capacitor voltage? → Q × V = 500 V. 1803 p 1803 · ⌂ Index

TNEB / TANGEDCO AE (EEE) — One Concept, Many Places 28 Stored energy — ½ × stiffness × (quantity)² Appears in: Circuits, Faults / stability / load flow, Synchronous machine, Utilisation, DC machine Capacitors, inductors and rotating masses all store energy with the same ½·k·x² form. W = ½CV² = Q²/2C (electric) , W = ½LI² (magnetic) , W = ½Jω² (rotating) , energy density ½εE², B²/2μ Where Same idea written there Remember Capacitor ½CV²; charge sharing between capacitors always loses energy Two equal C, one charged: half the energy is lost. Inductor ½LI²; breaking the current releases it as a spark / voltage spike Freewheeling diode gives it a safe path. Fields Electric ½εE² per m³, magnetic B²/(2μ) per m³ Force on a magnet ∝ B²·A/(2μ₀). Rotating machines ½Jω²; inertia constant H = ½Jω²/S (seconds) H of large alternators ≈ 2–9 s. Power-system stability Swing equation M d²δ/dt² = Pm − Pe with M = GH/(πf) Kinetic energy absorbs the accelerating power. Mechanics Spring ½kx²; flywheel ½Jω² Same squared form. ★ Memory hook: Every store is ½ × (C, L or J) × (V, I or ω)². Quick check — exam style Q. 100 µF charged to 200 V. Energy? → ½ × 100 µF × 200² = 2 J. Q. 0.5 H coil carrying 4 A. Energy? → ½ × 0.5 × 4² = 4 J. Q. 10 µF at 100 V joined to an equal uncharged 10 µF. Energy before and after? → 0.05 J → 0.025 J (half is lost in the connection). 1804 p 1804 · ⌂ Index

g.d: Every electrical idea as something you already know — current as water, voltage as pressure, and so on for each subject.
p: Analogy Book — see every electrical idea as something you already know The voltage is a pump, current is water flow, a resistor is a narrow pipe, a capacitor is a tank and an inductor is a heavy water wheel. This book gives a picture like that for 169 ideas across 19 subjects. Each card has the analogy, exactly how it matches the electrical behaviour, and the exam trap the picture helps you avoid. How to use it: before solving a sum, say the picture out loud ("tank filling through a narrow pipe"). The picture tells you what cannot jump, what grows, what decays and which way things flow. The master map — the water circuit Electrical Water / everyday Mechanical twin Voltage V pump pressure / height difference force Current I flow rate velocity Charge Q volume of water displacement Resistance R narrow pipe (friction) damper / friction Capacitance C tank (stores by height) spring (1/stiffness) Inductance L heavy wheel / water inertia mass Power P = VI pressure × flow force × velocity Energy ½CV² water held high spring energy ½kx² Energy ½LI² moving water kinetic energy ½mv² LC resonance U-tube sloshing mass on a spring TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1891 p 1891 · ⌂ Index

Contents 1. The water circuit — basic quantities 10 ideas 2. Circuit laws 10 ideas 3. Capacitor, inductor and transients 9 ideas 4. AC circuits 13 ideas 5. Three-phase 4 ideas 6. Magnetic circuits and transformers 12 ideas 7. DC machines 6 ideas 8. Induction and synchronous machines 7 ideas 9. Power systems 12 ideas 10. Protection and switchgear 7 ideas 11. Power electronics 10 ideas 12. Electronics 11 ideas 13. Control systems 7 ideas 14. Measurements 9 ideas 15. Electromagnetic fields 9 ideas 16. Digital electronics 9 ideas 17. Signals & DSP 8 ideas 18. Communication 8 ideas 19. Utilization of electrical energy 8 ideas TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1892 p 1892 · ⌂ Index

1. The water circuit — basic quantities Voltage (EMF, potential difference) · V · volt Picture it as: The PUMP (or the height difference between two tanks) PUMP = V narrow pipe = R water flow = current I (same all round a series loop) pressure drop across the narrow pipe: V = I × R How it matches: Pump pressure pushes water round the pipes; EMF pushes charge round the circuit. Voltage is always BETWEEN two points — like a height difference, never ‘at’ one point. Exam use / trap: Voltmeter goes ACROSS (like a pressure gauge with two hoses); a node has potential only relative to ground. Current · I · ampere Picture it as: WATER FLOW rate (litres per second) How it matches: Same flow passes every point of a single pipe — same current everywhere in a series loop. Exam use / trap: Ammeter goes IN SERIES (cut the pipe and insert a flow-meter). Charge · Q · coulomb Picture it as: The WATER itself (total litres) How it matches: Flow × time = litres; I × t = Q. Exam use / trap: Q = It (TNEB 2018 Q57: 10 A × 240 s = 2400 C). Resistance · R · ohm Picture it as: A NARROW or ROUGH PIPE How it matches: Long, thin pipes resist flow (R = ρL/A): longer pipe → more R, wider pipe → less R. Exam use / trap: Stretch a wire n times → length ×n, area ÷n → R × n². Conductance · G · siemens Picture it as: How WIDE / EASY the pipe is How it matches: G = 1/R — the opposite view of the same pipe. Exam use / trap: Parallel conductances simply add (like parallel pipes adding capacity). Power · P · watt Picture it as: Pump pressure × flow = how fast the pump does work How it matches: P = VI, like pressure × flow rate = hydraulic power. Exam use / trap: Same pipe (series) → use I²R; same pressure (parallel) → use V²/R. Energy · E · joule, kWh Picture it as: Total work done lifting water How it matches: Energy = power × time (E = Pt = VIt = QV). Exam use / trap: 1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 MJ. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1893 p 1893 · ⌂ Index

Ground / reference node · 0 V Picture it as: SEA LEVEL How it matches: All heights are measured from sea level; all node voltages from ground. Exam use / trap: Changing the reference changes every node voltage, never the differences. Short circuit · R = 0 Picture it as: A pipe with NO restriction (a bypass) How it matches: All flow takes the free path; no pressure drop across it (V = 0, I anything). Exam use / trap: Killed voltage source = short (pump removed, pipe joined). Open circuit · R = ∞ Picture it as: A CLOSED VALVE / blocked pipe How it matches: Pressure can exist across it but no flow (I = 0, V anything). Exam use / trap: Killed current source = open. Ideal voltmeter = open. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1894 p 1894 · ⌂ Index

2. Circuit laws Ohm's law · V = IR Picture it as: Pressure drop = flow × pipe narrowness How it matches: Push harder → more flow; narrower pipe → less flow for the same push. Exam use / trap: Holds for metals at constant temperature (not for diodes, arcs). KCL · ΣI = 0 Picture it as: Water entering a JUNCTION = water leaving How it matches: Water cannot pile up at a pipe joint; charge cannot pile up at a node. Exam use / trap: Charge conservation. KVL · ΣV = 0 Picture it as: Walk round a closed HILL path — total climb = total descent How it matches: Back at the start you are at the same height; round any loop the rises equal the drops. Exam use / trap: Energy conservation. Series · Rs = R1 + R2 Picture it as: Pipes JOINED END TO END How it matches: The same water passes both; each narrow section adds resistance. Exam use / trap: Series: same I, voltage divides in proportion to R. Parallel · 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 Picture it as: Pipes SIDE BY SIDE (more lanes on a road) How it matches: More lanes → easier flow → less total resistance, always below the smallest. Exam use / trap: Parallel: same V, current divides in INVERSE proportion to R. Voltage divider · Vout = V R2/(R1 + R2) Picture it as: Pressure shared by two pipe sections How it matches: The narrower section takes the bigger share of the pressure drop. Exam use / trap: Loading the output (connecting a load) lowers it. Thevenin equivalent · Vth, Rth Picture it as: A pump with a built-in narrow pipe, seen from the tap How it matches: Whatever the plumbing behind the tap, it looks like one pump (Vth) in series with one pipe (Rth). Exam use / trap: Rth: kill sources (pump → plain pipe, current source → closed valve). Superposition · — Picture it as: Two people pushing the same trolley How it matches: Effect of each pusher alone, added = total effect (only for linear systems). Exam use / trap: NOT valid for power (power ∝ I², not linear). Maximum power transfer · RL = Rth Picture it as: Water wheel loaded just right How it matches: Too little load: water rushes past doing nothing; too much: flow nearly stops. Best when load matches the source pipe. Exam use / trap: Efficiency at max power is only 50 %. Dependent source · — Picture it as: A pump whose speed is set by a sensor elsewhere How it matches: Its push depends on another flow/pressure in the circuit. Exam use / trap: Never ‘kill’ a dependent source when

3. Capacitor, inductor and transients Capacitor · C · farad Picture it as: A TANK (or a balloon / spring diaphragm) level = v_C TANK = capacitor C narrow pipe = R pump = source V Filling slows as the level rises: 63 % full at t = τ = RC, ~99 % at 5τ. The level cannot jump instantly → capacitor voltage is continuous. How it matches: Charging = filling the tank; the fuller it is, the harder it pushes back. A big tank (big C) needs more water (Q = CV) to rise 1 m. Exam use / trap: Voltage across C cannot JUMP (tank level can't change instantly). In DC steady state the full tank stops the flow → C = open. Inductor · L · henry Picture it as: A HEAVY WATER WHEEL / long pipe full of moving water (inertia) HEAVY WHEEL = inductor L flow = current i — the heavy wheel resists any CHANGE of flow shut the valve suddenly → water hammer (big voltage spike L di/dt) How it matches: Moving water resists any change in flow — it keeps going when the pump stops (water hammer). Exam use / trap: Current through L cannot JUMP. In DC steady state the wheel turns freely → L = short. Time constant RC · τ = RC Picture it as: Time to fill a tank through a narrow pipe How it matches: Bigger tank (C) or narrower pipe (R) → slower filling. After 1τ the tank is 63 % full, after 5τ practically full. Exam use / trap: Find t: t = τ ln(…) — take ln of the exponential. Time constant L/R · τ = L/R Picture it as: Time for a heavy wheel to spin up against friction How it matches: Heavier wheel (L) → slower; more friction (R) → settles faster (smaller τ). Exam use / trap: Note the INVERSE: more R makes RL faster but RC slower. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1896 p 1896 · ⌂ Index

Energy in C · ½CV² Picture it as: Water stored HIGH in the tank (potential energy) How it matches: Energy sits in the electric field like water held up. Exam use / trap: Halving V leaves ¼ of the energy. Energy in L · ½LI² Picture it as: Energy of the MOVING water (kinetic energy) How it matches: Energy is in the magnetic field like momentum in a moving mass. Exam use / trap: Opening an inductive circuit suddenly → huge spark (water hammer). LC oscillation · ω₀ = 1/√(LC) Picture it as: Water sloshing in a U-TUBE (or a pendulum, a mass on a spring) high side = C full low side moving water = L (current) Water sloshes left ↔ right: energy swaps between height (C) and motion (L) at ω₀ = 1/√(LC) How it matches: Tank (C) stores height energy, moving water (L) stores motion energy; energy swaps back and forth. Exam use / trap: With no R it rings for ever; R = friction makes it die out. Damping ratio ζ · ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) Picture it as: CAR SHOCK ABSORBER weak absorber: ζ < 1 (bounces) just right: ζ = 1 (no bounce) too stiff: ζ > 1 (slow) time → How it matches: Weak absorber → car bounces (underdamped); perfect → settles fastest with no bounce (critical); too stiff → slow crawl (overdamped). Exam use / trap: ζ < 1 oscillates; ζ = 1 critical; ζ > 1 sluggish. Initial value (t = 0⁺) · — Picture it as: Tank level / wheel speed just after the switch How it matches: Neither can change in zero time, so they equal their values just before switching. Exam use / trap: vC(0⁺) = vC(0⁻), iL(0⁺) = iL(0⁻). TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1897 p 1897 · ⌂ Index

4. AC circuits Alternating current · f · hertz Picture it as: A SAW cutting wood — back and forth, yet it still does work How it matches: Water sloshing to and fro in a pipe can still turn a paddle. Exam use / trap: Average of a full sine = 0, but power is not zero. RMS value · Vrms = Vm/√2 Picture it as: The STEADY push that would heat the same kettle How it matches: 230 V rms AC heats a heater exactly like 230 V DC. Exam use / trap: 230 V rms = 325 V peak. Meters read rms (MI) or average × 1.11 (PMMC rectifier). Phase / phase angle · φ Picture it as: Two children on SWINGS, one starting a little later How it matches: Same rhythm (frequency), different timing (phase). Exam use / trap: Compare phases only at the same frequency and same sin/cos reference. Reactance XL · XL = 2πfL Picture it as: Heavy wheel resists FAST back- and-forth more How it matches: Faster sloshing (higher f) → the inertia fights harder. Exam use / trap: XL ∝ f: zero at DC (short), huge at high f. Reactance XC · XC = 1/(2πfC) Picture it as: A rubber diaphragm in the pipe — easy for fast wiggles, blocks steady flow How it matches: Steady flow (DC) is stopped; fast back-and-forth passes easily. Exam use / trap: XC ∝ 1/f: open at DC, short at very high f. Impedance · Z = R + jX Picture it as: Total opposition = friction + inertia/spring effects How it matches: R wastes energy as heat; X only stores and returns it. Exam use / trap: |Z| = √(R² + X²); angle = tan⁻¹(X/R). Power factor · pf = cos φ Picture it as: A HORSE pulling a barge from the river bank at an angle canal barge horse on the bank (S) useful pull = P sideways = Q pf = cos φ = P/S How it matches: Only the pull along the canal moves the barge (real power); the sideways pull is wasted effort (reactive). Exam use / trap: Low pf → more current for the same useful power → bigger losses and cables. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1898 p 1898 · ⌂ Index

Real, reactive, apparent power · P, Q, S Picture it as: A glass of BEER: liquid = P, foam = Q, whole glass = S foam = Q (kVAr) beer = P (kW) whole glass = S (kVA) S² = P² + Q² How it matches: You pay for the whole glass (S) but drink only the beer (P). S² = P² + Q². Exam use / trap: kW does work; kVAr only sloshes back and forth; kVA sizes the equipment. pf correction (capacitor) · Qc = P(tan φ1 − tan φ2) Picture it as: Letting a SECOND horse pull from the other bank How it matches: The sideways pulls cancel, so less total effort for the same forward motion. Exam use / trap: Capacitor supplies kVAr locally; motors draw lagging kVAr. Resonance · XL = XC Picture it as: Pushing a SWING at exactly its natural rhythm small push exactly in step pushing at the natural frequency f₀ builds a huge swing = RESONANCE (high Q) How it matches: Small pushes in step build a huge swing; series resonance gives max current, parallel gives min current. Exam use / trap: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)); Q factor = how high the swing builds. Q factor / bandwidth · Q = f₀/BW Picture it as: A wine glass that rings for a long time (sharp tuning) How it matches: High Q → rings long and responds only near one frequency (narrow bandwidth). Exam use / trap: R raises losses → lowers Q → wider band. Coupled coils / mutual inductance · M = k√(L1L2) Picture it as: Two water wheels on ONE shared axle (or two gears in mesh) How it matches: Turning one drives the other; how tightly they are linked is k (0 to 1). Exam use / trap: Aiding +2M (both currents into the dots), opposing −2M. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1899 p 1899 · ⌂ Index

Reflected impedance · (ωM)²/Z2 Picture it as: A load on the second wheel makes the first wheel feel heavier How it matches: Whatever the secondary carries is felt back on the primary. Exam use / trap: Zin = Z1 + (ωM)²/Z2. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1900 p 1900 · ⌂ Index

5. Three-phase Three-phase supply · 120° apart Picture it as: THREE CYCLISTS on one crank, pedals 120° apart How it matches: Someone is always pushing hard, so the shaft gets smooth, constant power. Exam use / trap: Balanced 3-φ: instantaneous total power is constant. Neutral current · In = 0 (balanced) Picture it as: Three equal pushes at 120° cancel exactly How it matches: Like three equal ropes pulling a ring at 120° — the ring does not move. Exam use / trap: Unbalanced load → neutral current flows; broken neutral → voltage shift. Star vs delta · VL = √3 Vph (Y), IL = √3 Iph (Δ) Picture it as: Star = meeting at a common hub; delta = holding hands in a ring How it matches: Star adds two phases at 120° → √3 more voltage between lines; delta splits line current between two phases. Exam use / trap: Star–delta starter cuts starting current to ⅓. Phase sequence · RYB Picture it as: The ORDER in which cyclists push How it matches: Swap any two and the shaft turns the other way. Exam use / trap: Swapping two supply lines reverses an induction motor. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1901 p 1901 · ⌂ Index

6. Magnetic circuits and transformers Magnetic flux · Φ · weber Picture it as: WATER FLOW in a magnetic ‘pipe’ (the iron core) How it matches: MMF pushes flux round the core like a pump pushes water. Exam use / trap: Φ = MMF/reluctance — the ‘Ohm's law’ of magnetism. MMF · NI · ampere-turn Picture it as: The PUMP of the magnetic circuit How it matches: More turns or more current → more push for flux. Reluctance · S = l/(μA) Picture it as: Narrow pipe for flux; an AIR GAP is like a sudden clogged section How it matches: Even a small air gap dominates the total reluctance (air μ is ~1000× lower). Exam use / trap: Machines need much more magnetising current than transformers because of the air gap. Hysteresis · Ph ∝ f B^1.6 Picture it as: Bending a paper-clip back and forth — it warms up How it matches: Magnetic domains flipping every cycle waste energy as heat. Exam use / trap: ∝ f; reduced by silicon steel (narrow loop). Eddy currents · Pe ∝ f²B²t² Picture it as: Little WHIRLPOOLS in a river How it matches: Circulating currents in solid iron waste energy; slicing the core (laminations) breaks the whirlpools. Exam use / trap: ∝ f² and ∝ thickness²: laminate thin. Transformer · V1/V2 = N1/N2 Picture it as: A LEVER (or bicycle gears) long arm: big movement, small force short arm: small movement, big Transformer: high V ↔ low I, low V ↔ high I V₁I₁ = V₂I₂ (power same, like work in = work out) How it matches: Trade force for distance: step voltage up → current goes down by the same ratio; power stays the same. Exam use / trap: Works only on AC (changing flux). DC gives no output, and burns the winding. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1902 p 1902 · ⌂ Index

Referring impedance · Z′ = a²Z Picture it as: Looking at a load through a gearbox How it matches: Through gears the load ‘feels’ heavier or lighter by the ratio squared. Exam use / trap: Refer to HV side: multiply by a²; to LV side: divide. Open-circuit / short-circuit test · Pi, Pcu Picture it as: Engine idling (fuel just to keep running) vs. braking at full load How it matches: OC test at rated V shows core (idling) loss; SC test at rated I shows copper (load) loss. Exam use / trap: OC on LV side, SC on HV side. Maximum efficiency · Cu loss = iron loss Picture it as: A shop whose fixed rent equals its variable costs How it matches: Below that load the fixed cost dominates; above it the variable cost grows as x². Exam use / trap: x = √(Pi/Pcu,FL). Voltage regulation · (E − V)/V Picture it as: Water pressure falling at the far tap when many taps are open How it matches: Internal drop I(R cos φ + X sin φ) lowers the terminal voltage on load. Exam use / trap: Leading pf can make regulation negative. Current transformer · secondary never open Picture it as: A water hose kinked under full pump pressure How it matches: Primary current is forced by the line; opening the secondary removes the opposing flux → dangerous high voltage. Exam use / trap: Always short a CT secondary before removing the meter. Autotransformer · one shared winding Picture it as: A STEP-LADDER instead of two separate ladders How it matches: Part of the same winding serves both sides, so less copper. Exam use / trap: No isolation between primary and secondary. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1903 p 1903 · ⌂ Index

7. DC machines DC motor · T = kΦIa Picture it as: A water wheel turned by a pressure jet How it matches: Current in a magnetic field gets a push (motor action). Exam use / trap: Torque ∝ flux × armature current. Back EMF · Eb = V − IaRa Picture it as: A water wheel acting as a pump against the supply as it speeds up How it matches: Faster spin → more back-push → less current. At start Eb = 0 → huge current (needs a starter). Exam use / trap: Eb ∝ ΦN. Speed vs field · N ∝ Eb/Φ Picture it as: A cyclist on an easier gear spins faster How it matches: Weaker field → needs to spin faster to make the same back EMF. Exam use / trap: Field circuit open on a shunt motor → dangerous over-speed. Series motor · T ∝ Ia² Picture it as: A tug-boat — huge pull from standstill How it matches: High starting torque (traction, cranes); runs away with no load. Exam use / trap: Never start a series motor without load. Commutator · — Picture it as: A ROTATING SWITCH that flips connections each half turn How it matches: Keeps the torque in one direction by reversing coil current at the right moment. Armature reaction · — Picture it as: A strong cross-wind bending a fountain jet How it matches: Armature flux distorts and weakens the main field. Exam use / trap: Interpoles and compensating windings correct it. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1904 p 1904 · ⌂ Index

8. Induction and synchronous machines Rotating magnetic field · Ns = 120f/P Picture it as: A STADIUM WAVE running round the crowd How it matches: Three phases in turn create a field that travels round the stator. Exam use / trap: Swap two phases → wave runs the other way. Slip · s = (Ns − N)/Ns Picture it as: A SURFER always a little behind the wave surfer = rotor (N) wave = rotating field (Ns) The surfer always lags the wave a little: slip s = (Ns − N)/Ns How it matches: If the rotor caught the field there would be no relative motion, no induced current, no torque. Exam use / trap: Rotor frequency = s·f; at standstill s = 1. Induction motor torque–slip · Tmax at s = R2/X2 Picture it as: Dragging a boat with a rope through water How it matches: Small slip: torque ∝ s; large slip: rotor reactance makes torque fall. Exam use / trap: Adding rotor resistance moves Tmax to higher slip (more starting torque). Synchronous machine load angle · P = (EV/X) sin δ Picture it as: A DOG ON A LEASH beside its owner owner = rotor (E) dog = bus (V) δ same speed, angle grows with load; past 90° the leash slips (out of step) How it matches: Both run at the same speed; harder pull → bigger angle δ; past 90° the leash slips (loss of synchronism). Exam use / trap: Pmax at δ = 90°. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1905 p 1905 · ⌂ Index

Over/under excitation · — Picture it as: Adjusting how hard the dog leans sideways How it matches: Over-excited synchronous motor supplies kVAr (works like a capacitor); under-excited draws kVAr. Exam use / trap: Synchronous condenser = over- excited motor on no load. Synchronising (paralleling) · same V, f, phase, sequence Picture it as: Jumping onto a moving merry-go- round How it matches: Match speed and position first, then step on smoothly. Exam use / trap: Dark-lamp / synchroscope method. Single-phase induction motor · needs auxiliary winding Picture it as: A pendulum pushed straight — it swings but chooses no direction How it matches: A single winding gives a pulsating field (two equal opposite waves) → no starting torque. Exam use / trap: Capacitor-start adds a second phase-shifted field. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1906 p 1906 · ⌂ Index

9. Power systems Transmission at high voltage · loss = I²R Picture it as: Sending water through pipes at HIGH PRESSURE, LOW FLOW How it matches: Same power with less current → much less friction loss in long pipes. Exam use / trap: Double the voltage → quarter the loss. Power flow P = V1V2 sin δ / X · δ Picture it as: Water flows from the HIGHER tank to the lower (angle = height) How it matches: Real power flows from the leading angle to the lagging; reactive power flows from higher V to lower V. Exam use / trap: Pmax = V1V2/X at 90°. Voltage drop / reactive power · Q ↔ V Picture it as: Pressure falling at the end of a long pipe How it matches: Reactive power support (capacitors) props up the pressure (voltage) locally. Exam use / trap: Q controls V; P controls f and δ. Ferranti effect · Vr > Vs on light load Picture it as: A water-hammer / sloshing rise at the dead end of a long pipe How it matches: Line charging current through line inductance raises the far-end voltage at no load. Exam use / trap: Long lines on light load; shunt reactors fix it. Frequency & load balance · f ↔ P Picture it as: Keeping a bicycle's speed steady going up and down hills How it matches: More load (uphill) → generators slow (f falls) until governors add more steam/water. Exam use / trap: Droop: Δf ∝ ΔP. Inertia constant H · H = stored KE / rating Picture it as: A heavy FLYWHEEL that resists speed change How it matches: Bigger H → frequency changes more slowly after a disturbance. Exam use / trap: Swing equation M d²δ/dt² = Pm − Pe. Transient stability (equal area) · A1 = A2 Picture it as: A ball rolling in a valley, kicked by a fault How it matches: Energy gained during the fault (A1) must be given back before it rolls over the hill (A2). Exam use / trap: Clear faults fast → smaller A1. Per-unit system · pu = actual/base Picture it as: Marks out of 100 instead of raw marks How it matches: Everything on one common scale, so transformer ratios disappear. Exam use / trap: Zbase = kV²/MVA. Short-circuit fault · If = E/Z Picture it as: A pipe BURSTING straight to the drain How it matches: Flow is limited only by the pipe narrowness up to the break → enormous current. Exam use / trap: 3-φ fault is usually the largest; LG most common. Symmetrical components · +, −, 0 sequence Picture it as: Breaking an untidy push into three neat patterns How it matches: Any unbalanced set = a forward

Earthing · low earth resistance Picture it as: A big DRAIN to the ground How it matches: Fault current has an easy path away, so touching the body stays safe. Exam use / trap: Earth resistance should be low (≤ 1 Ω substations). Corona · above disruptive voltage Picture it as: Air ‘boiling’ around a too-thin, too-highly-stressed wire How it matches: Air near the conductor ionises: hissing, glow, loss, radio noise. Exam use / trap: Bundled / thicker conductors reduce it. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1908 p 1908 · ⌂ Index

10. Protection and switchgear Fuse · — Picture it as: The WEAKEST LINK in a chain How it matches: It breaks deliberately to save everything else. Exam use / trap: Has to be replaced after operating. Circuit breaker · — Picture it as: A TAP that can shut under full flow and be reopened How it matches: Opens contacts and quenches the arc; reusable. Exam use / trap: Arc quenching media: air, oil, SF₆, vacuum. Relay · — Picture it as: A WATCHMAN who rings the bell for the breaker How it matches: Senses abnormal current/voltage and tells the breaker to trip. Exam use / trap: Relay detects; breaker interrupts. IDMT relay · t ∝ 1/(PSM^0.02 − 1) Picture it as: A guard who reacts faster to bigger trouble How it matches: Large fault → quick trip; small overload → slow trip. Exam use / trap: Grading: upstream relay waits a margin longer. Differential protection · Iin = Iout Picture it as: Counting people entering and leaving a hall How it matches: If the counts differ, someone is trapped inside → internal fault. Exam use / trap: Through faults do not trip it. Distance relay · Z = V/I Picture it as: Estimating how far a thunderclap is from the flash-to-sound time How it matches: Measured impedance tells how far away the fault is. Exam use / trap: Zones 1-2-3 cover more line with more delay. Lightning arrester · — Picture it as: A pressure-relief VALVE How it matches: Stays shut at normal voltage, opens to bleed a surge to earth, then closes. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1909 p 1909 · ⌂ Index

11. Power electronics Diode · — Picture it as: A NON-RETURN VALVE How it matches: Lets flow pass one way only. Exam use / trap: Forward drop ≈ 0.7 V (Si); reverse = blocks. SCR (thyristor) · — Picture it as: A LATCHING DOOR that opens on a knock and stays open while people pass How it matches: A gate pulse turns it on; it stays on until current falls below holding current. Exam use / trap: Gate can't turn it off (except GTO). MOSFET / IGBT switch · — Picture it as: A TAP that can be opened and closed on command, very fast How it matches: Fully controlled switches for choppers and inverters. Exam use / trap: MOSFET fastest, IGBT for higher power. Rectifier · AC → DC Picture it as: A NON-RETURN VALVE on a sloshing pipe How it matches: Lets only one direction through, so the average flow moves one way. Exam use / trap: Full-wave Vavg = 2Vm/π. Firing angle α · Vdc ∝ cos α Picture it as: Opening a SLUICE GATE later in each wave How it matches: The later you open, the less water gets through each cycle. Exam use / trap: α > 90° → average reverses (inverter mode). Filter capacitor · ripple Picture it as: A WATER TANK smoothing a pulsing supply How it matches: Stores water at the peaks and supplies it between them. Exam use / trap: Bigger C or load current smaller → less ripple. Buck converter · Vo = DVs Picture it as: A tap switched ON and OFF quickly — the average flow is less How it matches: On for D of the time → average pressure D·Vs (the inductor smooths it). Boost converter · Vo = Vs/(1 − D) Picture it as: A HYDRAULIC RAM pump — the moving water's momentum lifts water higher How it matches: The inductor builds momentum while shorted, then forces it out at a higher voltage. Exam use / trap: D → 1 gives very high gain (in theory). Inverter · DC → AC Picture it as: Two people alternately pushing a door from each side How it matches: Switches reverse the connection to make alternating output. Exam use / trap: PWM shapes it towards a sine. Freewheeling diode · — Picture it as: A bypass pipe that lets moving water keep circulating How it matches: Gives inductive current a path when the switch opens, avoiding a voltage spike. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1910 p 1910 · ⌂ Index

12. Electronics Semiconductor doping · n/p type Picture it as: A queue with extra people (n) or empty seats moving along (p, holes) How it matches: Electrons are the extra people; holes are gaps that appear to move the other way. PN junction / depletion layer · — Picture it as: A no-man's-land between two crowds How it matches: Forward bias shrinks it (crowds pushed together); reverse bias widens it. Zener diode · Vz Picture it as: An overflow WEIR — water above the edge spills away How it matches: Holds the voltage at Vz by passing whatever extra current is needed. Exam use / trap: Used as a voltage regulator in reverse breakdown. BJT transistor · Ic = βIb Picture it as: A small hand turning a big WATER TAP How it matches: A small base current controls a much larger collector current. Exam use / trap: Saturation = tap fully open; cut-off = closed. FET · voltage-controlled Picture it as: A gate valve moved by PRESSURE, not flow How it matches: Gate voltage controls the channel with almost no gate current (very high input impedance). Amplifier gain · A = Vout/Vin Picture it as: A MEGAPHONE How it matches: Small input, bigger copy at the output, using power from a supply. Exam use / trap: Gain in dB = 20 log(V ratio). Negative feedback · A/(1 + Aβ) Picture it as: A driver correcting the steering continuously How it matches: Compares output with target and corrects → stable, accurate, less distortion, lower gain. Exam use / trap: Gain × bandwidth stays constant. Op-amp (ideal) · V+ = V− Picture it as: A servant who adjusts the output until both inputs are equal How it matches: With negative feedback it forces the virtual short; inputs draw no current. Exam use / trap: Inverting gain −Rf/Rin. Oscillator · Aβ = 1 Picture it as: A SWING kept going by tiny pushes in step How it matches: Positive feedback in phase replaces the energy lost each cycle. Exam use / trap: Barkhausen: loop gain 1, phase 0°/360°. Logic gates · AND / OR Picture it as: AND = two switches in SERIES (both must close); OR = in PARALLEL How it matches: A lamp lights only if both (AND) or either (OR) switch is closed. Exam use / trap: NAND/NOR are universal. Flip-flop · 1-bit memory Picture it as: A LIGHT SWITCH that stays where you left it How it matches: Holds its state until told to change. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1911 p 1911 · ⌂ Index

13. Control systems Open loop vs closed loop · — Picture it as: Toaster timer vs room THERMOSTAT How it matches: Open loop does not check the result; closed loop measures and corrects. Exam use / trap: Closed loop: accurate, can become unstable. Steady-state error · ess Picture it as: A cruise control that settles slightly below the set speed How it matches: Proportional control alone leaves an offset; integral action removes it. Exam use / trap: Type of system decides which inputs give zero error. PID controller · P, I, D Picture it as: Driving: P = how far from the lane centre, I = how long you have drifted, D = how fast you are drifting How it matches: Combine all three for a smooth, accurate, quick correction. Exam use / trap: D reduces overshoot; I removes offset. Overshoot & settling · Mp, ts Picture it as: Parking a car — overshoot the spot and come back How it matches: Low damping = big overshoot and long settling. Exam use / trap: Mp depends only on ζ. Stability · poles in LHP Picture it as: A ball in a BOWL (stable) vs on top of a hill (unstable) How it matches: Disturbed, the stable ball returns; the unstable one runs away. Exam use / trap: Any RHP pole → unstable. Gain & phase margin · GM, PM Picture it as: How far a car is from the cliff edge How it matches: Safety distance before the loop starts to oscillate. Exam use / trap: PM 30–60° gives good damping. Transport lag · e^(−sT) Picture it as: Shower with a long pipe — you turn the tap, the hot water arrives later How it matches: Delay adds phase lag without changing gain → can destabilise. Exam use / trap: Phase = −ωT rad. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1912 p 1912 · ⌂ Index

14. Measurements Ammeter · series, low R Picture it as: A FLOW METER cut into the pipe How it matches: Must not restrict the flow, so very low resistance. Exam use / trap: Connected across a supply it acts as a short. Voltmeter · parallel, high R Picture it as: A PRESSURE GAUGE tapped across two points How it matches: Must not leak water, so very high resistance. Shunt (ammeter range extension) · Rsh = Rm/(m − 1) Picture it as: A BYPASS pipe taking most of the flow How it matches: Only a known small share passes through the meter. Multiplier (voltmeter range) · Rse = Rm(m − 1) Picture it as: A long narrow pipe in series with the gauge How it matches: Drops most of the pressure before the gauge. Wheatstone bridge · R1R4 = R2R3 Picture it as: A BALANCE SCALE How it matches: At balance no current flows through the galvanometer (the scale is level). Exam use / trap: Null method → very accurate. PMMC instrument · reads average Picture it as: A weather-vane that points to the AVERAGE wind How it matches: Pure AC averages to zero, so it reads 0 without a rectifier. Exam use / trap: DC only (or with rectifier, scaled by 1.11). Moving-iron instrument · reads rms Picture it as: Two iron pieces that repel whichever way the current flows How it matches: Deflection ∝ I², so it reads AC and DC (rms). Energy meter · revolutions ∝ kWh Picture it as: A water meter wheel counting litres How it matches: The disc turns at a speed ∝ power, so total turns ∝ energy. Exam use / trap: Meter constant = rev/kWh. CRO · — Picture it as: A pen drawing on moving paper How it matches: Horizontal sweep = time, vertical deflection = signal. Exam use / trap: Lissajous patterns compare frequencies. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1913 p 1913 · ⌂ Index

15. Electromagnetic fields Electric potential · V · volt Picture it as: HEIGHT on a hill How it matches: Equipotential lines are contour lines; moving along a contour costs no work. Exam use / trap: Field lines always cross equipotentials at right angles. Electric field · E · V/m Picture it as: The SLOPE of the hill (field points downhill) How it matches: E = −dV/dx: a steep slope is a strong field. Between parallel plates the slope is constant, E = V/d. Exam use / trap: 1 kV across 1 mm = 10⁶ V/m. Gauss's law (electric flux) · ∮D·dS = Q Picture it as: Water flowing out of a closed bag = the tap inside it How it matches: Total flux out of any closed surface equals the charge enclosed, whatever the bag's shape. Exam use / trap: No charge inside → net flux zero. Permittivity (dielectric) · ε = ε₀εr Picture it as: A SPONGE that holds more water per unit pressure How it matches: A dielectric lets the plates hold more charge per volt: C = εA/d grows with εr. Exam use / trap: Inserting a dielectric (battery connected) raises Q; (battery removed) lowers V. Magnetic field round a wire · B = μ₀I/(2πr) Picture it as: WATER SWIRLING round a drain How it matches: The swirl circles the current (right- hand grip) and weakens as 1/r. Exam use / trap: Inside a solid wire B rises with r; outside it falls as 1/r. Displacement current · Id = ε A dE/dt Picture it as: Water pushing an ELASTIC MEMBRANE in a pipe How it matches: No water crosses the membrane, yet flow continues on both sides — current 'through' a capacitor. Exam use / trap: Makes Ampère's law hold at a capacitor (Maxwell). Skin effect · δ = √(2/(ωμσ)) Picture it as: Rain RUN-OFF stays on the surface How it matches: AC crowds to the outer skin of a conductor; higher frequency → thinner skin → higher Rac. Exam use / trap: Hollow / stranded conductors at high current or frequency. Method of images · — Picture it as: A MIRROR How it matches: A charge above a grounded plane acts as if an opposite charge sits at its mirror point below. Exam use / trap: Force on the charge = q²/(4πε₀(2h)²). Electromagnetic wave · η₀ = 377 Ω Picture it as: A STADIUM WAVE How it matches: E and H hand energy back and forth while the pattern travels at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀). Exam use / trap: E/H = 377 Ω in free space. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1914 p 1914 · ⌂ Index

16. Digital electronics AND / OR gate · Y = A·B, A + B Picture it as: Two SWITCHES in series / in parallel How it matches: Lamp lights only if both series switches close (AND) or if either parallel switch closes (OR). Exam use / trap: NAND and NOR alone can build any gate (universal). Inverter · Y = Ā Picture it as: A SEE-SAW How it matches: One end up means the other end down. Exam use / trap: Two inverters in series give the input back. Latch / flip-flop · 1 bit of memory Picture it as: A LIGHT SWITCH that stays where you leave it How it matches: It keeps its state after your hand leaves — memory. Exam use / trap: SR: S = R = 1 is the forbidden input. T (toggle) flip-flop · Q⁺ = Q̄ when T = 1 Picture it as: A PUSH-BUTTON lamp: press on, press off How it matches: Each clock with T = 1 flips the state — a divide-by-2 circuit. Exam use / trap: n toggling flip-flops divide the clock by 2ⁿ. Clock · fclk Picture it as: A CONDUCTOR'S BATON How it matches: Every synchronous flip-flop changes only on the beat. Exam use / trap: Synchronous counter: all stages share one clock. Ripple counter · delay = n·tpd Picture it as: DOMINOES falling one after another How it matches: Each stage waits for the previous one, so delays add up. Exam use / trap: Max clock ≈ 1/(n·tpd). Shift register · SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO Picture it as: A BUCKET BRIGADE How it matches: Each clock passes every bit one place along the line. Exam use / trap: n-bit serial-in → output after n clocks. Multiplexer / demultiplexer · 2ⁿ inputs, n select lines Picture it as: A RAILWAY JUNCTION How it matches: Select lines set the points: one of many tracks joins the main line (MUX), or the main line feeds one of many (DEMUX). Exam use / trap: A 2ⁿ:1 MUX can realise any n- variable function. Tri-state buffer · 0, 1, high-Z Picture it as: A door that can be OPEN, CLOSED or TAKEN AWAY How it matches: High-Z disconnects the output so many devices can share one bus. Exam use / trap: Used on data buses. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1915 p 1915 · ⌂ Index

17. Signals & DSP Impulse response · h(t), h[n] Picture it as: CLAP ONCE and record the hall's reply How it matches: The reply to one sharp clap describes the whole room (LTI system). Exam use / trap: Knowing h gives the output for any input. Convolution · y = x * h Picture it as: ECHOES in a hall How it matches: The output is every past input, each followed by its own echo pattern, all added up. Exam use / trap: Convolution in time = multiplication in frequency. Fourier series / spectrum · harmonics Picture it as: A PRISM splitting white light into colours How it matches: Any periodic wave splits into sine waves of f, 2f, 3f … Exam use / trap: Square wave → only odd harmonics. Sampling & aliasing · fs ≥ 2fmax Picture it as: FILM FRAMES — wagon wheels that seem to turn backwards How it matches: Too few frames per turn and the wheel's true speed is disguised as a slower one. Exam use / trap: Alias at |f − k·fs|. Low-pass filter · fc = 1/(2πRC) Picture it as: CAR SUSPENSION smoothing out bumps How it matches: Slow changes pass, fast jolts are absorbed. Exam use / trap: RC = 1 s → fc ≈ 0.16 Hz. Stability (BIBO) · poles in LHP / inside |z| = 1 Picture it as: A BALL IN A BOWL vs a ball on a HILLTOP How it matches: Disturb the bowl and the ball settles (stable); on the hilltop it rolls away (unstable). Exam use / trap: One pole in the right half-plane → unstable. Delay z⁻¹ · y[n] = x[n − 1] Picture it as: A one-step QUEUE How it matches: Each sample waits one tick before moving on. Exam use / trap: z⁻ᵏ = delay of k samples. Causality · h(t) = 0 for t < 0 Picture it as: No one can REPLY BEFORE BEING ASKED How it matches: A real-time system cannot use future inputs. Exam use / trap: Ideal (brick-wall) filters are non- causal. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1916 p 1916 · ⌂ Index

18. Communication Carrier & modulation · fc ≫ fm Picture it as: A TRUCK carrying the message as cargo How it matches: The low-frequency message rides on a high-frequency carrier that antennas can launch. Exam use / trap: Antenna length ≈ λ/2 — impossible at audio frequencies. AM vs FM · m, β Picture it as: LOUDNESS change vs PITCH change (a siren) How it matches: AM varies the carrier's size; FM varies its frequency. Exam use / trap: FM resists noise because noise mostly disturbs amplitude. Bandwidth & capacity · C = B log₂(1 + SNR) Picture it as: LANES on a highway How it matches: More lanes (bandwidth) and a clearer road (SNR) carry more traffic (bits per second). Exam use / trap: SNR 1000 (30 dB), B = 3 kHz → C ≈ 30 kb/s. Noise & SNR · SNR (dB) Picture it as: TALKING in a noisy room How it matches: What matters is how much louder the voice is than the crowd. Exam use / trap: Noise figure F = SNRin/SNRout ≥ 1. FDM vs TDM · — Picture it as: RADIO STATIONS on different channels vs people TAKING TURNS to speak How it matches: FDM shares the band at once; TDM shares the time slot by slot. Exam use / trap: TDM is natural for digital (PCM) signals. Superheterodyne receiver · IF = 455 kHz (AM) Picture it as: TRANSLATING every language into one common language first How it matches: Every station is shifted to one fixed IF so one well-tuned amplifier does the work. Exam use / trap: Image frequency = fs + 2·IF. Pre-emphasis / de-emphasis · 75 µs (FM) Picture it as: SPEAKING the soft high notes louder before a noisy line How it matches: High audio frequencies are boosted at the transmitter and cut back at the receiver, cutting the noise with them. Exam use / trap: Improves FM SNR at high audio frequencies. Antenna · λ/2 dipole Picture it as: A TUNING FORK How it matches: It radiates best at the frequency its length matches. Exam use / trap: λ = c/f: 100 MHz → 3 m, half-wave dipole ≈ 1.5 m. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1917 p 1917 · ⌂ Index

19. Utilization of electrical energy Luminous intensity · illuminance · cd · lux = lm/m² Picture it as: A TORCH's brightness in one direction · RAIN per square metre How it matches: Candela is how strongly a source shines one way; lux is how much light lands on each square metre. Exam use / trap: E = I/d² (inverse square) and E = I cos θ/d² (cosine law). Inverse-square law · E ∝ 1/d² Picture it as: SPRAY PAINT thinning out with distance How it matches: Twice as far → the same paint covers 4 times the area. Exam use / trap: Lamp raised from 2 m to 4 m → illuminance ¼. Resistance heating · P = I²R Picture it as: FRICTION in a narrow pipe How it matches: Forcing current through resistance turns energy into heat. Exam use / trap: Nichrome elements: high ρ, no oxidation. Induction heating · eddy currents Picture it as: WHIRLPOOLS stirred inside the metal How it matches: An AC coil induces swirling currents that heat the work-piece from inside; higher f → shallower heating. Exam use / trap: Used for surface hardening and melting. Dielectric heating · P ∝ f V² tan δ Picture it as: MOLECULES jostling back and forth How it matches: Polar molecules twist with the field many million times a second and warm up (like a microwave oven). Exam use / trap: Heats insulators — wood, plastics, food. Train speed–time curve · accelerate, free-run, coast, brake Picture it as: A BUS between two stops How it matches: Speed up, cruise, roll on, then brake — the area under the curve is the distance. Exam use / trap: Shorter runs → no free-running part (trapezoidal curve). Regenerative braking · motor → generator Picture it as: A PUMP run backwards as a TURBINE downhill How it matches: The motor slows the train and sends energy back to the supply. Exam use / trap: Works only when the back EMF exceeds the supply voltage. Battery capacity · Ah · Wh = V × Ah Picture it as: A WATER TANK: size = Ah, height = volts How it matches: Stored energy = how much water × how high it sits. Exam use / trap: 12 V, 100 Ah = 1.2 kWh. TNEB AE (EEE) — Analogy Book 1918 p 1918 · ⌂ Index

g.d: Capacitor and inductor charging and discharging explained simply in Tamil, with the three compared.
p: RC · RL · RLC — தமிழில் எளிய விளக்கம் Capacitor எப்படி charge / discharge ஆகிறது, inductor-ல் current ஏன் உடனே மாறாது, RLC ஏன் ஊஞ்சல் மாதிரி ஆடுகிறது — இவை அனைத்தையும் தண்ணீர் டேங்க், குழாய், U-குழாய் கதைகள் மூலம், கணக்கிட்ட வளைவுப் படங்களுடன் (curves) விளக்குகிறோம். கடைசியில் மூன்றையும் ஒப்பிடும் அட்டவணையும், GATE மாதிரி கணக்குகளும் (விடையுடன்) உள்ளன. பகுதி என்ன இருக்கிறது 1 · RC டேங்க் கதை, charging / discharging வளைவு, τ = RC, நேரம் கண்டுபிடிப்பது (ln) 2 · RL நீண்ட குழாய் கதை, current ஏறுதல் / இறங்குதல், τ = L/R, voltage spike 3 · RLC U-குழாய் ஊஞ்சல் கதை, over / critical / under damping, resonance, Q, bandwidth 4 · ஒப்பீடு RC vs RL vs RLC ஒரே அட்டவணையில், 0⁺ / ∞ நடத்தை, √(L/C) குடும்பம் 5 · மாதிரி கணக்குகள் GATE மாதிரி 20 கணக்குகள் (ஆங்கிலத்தில், தீர்வு + trap) TNEB AE (EEE) — RC · RL · RLC (Tamil) 1919 p 1919 · ⌂ Index

பகுதி 1 · RC — டேங்க் நிரம்பும் கதை கதை: ஒரு பம்ப் (supply V) ஒரு குறுகிய குழாய் (R) வழியாக ஒரு டேங்கை (C) நிரப்புகிறது. டேங்க் காலியாக இருக்கும்போது பம்புக்கும் டேங்குக்கும் உள்ள வித்தியாசம் அதிகம் → நீர் வேகமாக பாயும். டேங்க் நிரம்ப நிரம்ப வித்தியாசம் குறையும் → பாய்வு மெதுவாகும். அதனால்தான் charging முதலில் வேகமாக, பிறகு மெதுவாக — ஒரு வளைவு (curve). பம்ப் = V (supply) R = குழாய் (குறுகலானது) நீர் மட்டம் = vC டேங்க் = C (capacitor) வித்தியாசம் அதிகம் → பாய்வு (current) அதிகம் தொடக்கம்: டேங்க் காலி பம்ப் = V (supply) R = குழாய் (குறுகலானது) நீர் மட்டம் = vC டேங்க் = C (capacitor) வித்தியாசம் குறைவு → பாய்வு மிகக் குறைவு பின்பு: டேங்க் கிட்டத்தட்ட நிரம்பியது மின்சாரம் தண்ணீர் கதை Voltage vC டேங்கில் உள்ள நீர் மட்டம் Current i குழாயில் பாயும் நீர் அளவு Resistance R குழாய் எவ்வளவு குறுகலானது (குறுகல் அதிகம் = மெதுவான ஓட்டம்) Capacitance C டேங்கின் அகலம் (அகலம் அதிகம் = நிரப்ப நேரம் அதிகம்) Time constant τ = R × C (seconds) R பெரிது அல்லது C பெரிது → τ பெரிது → மெதுவான charging. உதாரணம்: R = 1 kΩ, C = 100 μF → τ = 0.1 s. Charging (சார்ஜ் ஆவது): v = V (1 − e−t/τ) TNEB AE (EEE) — RC · RL · RLC (Tamil) 1920 p 1920 · ⌂ Index

0 1 2 3 4 5 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1 t / τ பின்னம் (fraction) 63.2 % 99.3 % 36.8 % vC / V (charging) i / I₀ (current) Charging: voltage ஏறுகிறது (நீல வளைவு); current இறங்குகிறது (சிவப்பு) Discharging (டிஸ்சார்ஜ் ஆவது): v = V₀ e−t/τ பம்பை அணைத்து, டேங்கின் அடியில் உள்ள குழாயைத் திறக்கிறோம். நீர் அதிகம் இருக்கும்போது அழுத்தம் அதிகம் → வேகமாக வெளியேறும்; பிறகு மெதுவாகும். 0 1 2 3 4 5 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1 t / τ பின்னம் 36.8 % 5 % vC / V₀ (discharging) Discharging: முதலில் வேகமாக, பிறகு மெதுவாக இறங்குகிறது நேரம் Charging — ஏறியது Discharging — மீதி 1τ 63.2 % 36.8 % 2τ 86.5 % 13.5 % 3τ 95.0 % 5.0 % 4τ 98.2 % 1.8 % 5τ 99.3 % 0.7 % ஞாபகம்: 1τ → 63 % ஏறும் / 37 % மீதி · 3τ → 95 % · 5τ → ஏறக்குறைய முழுமை (99.3 %). ஏறியது + மீதி = 100 %. "இவ்வளவு volt வர எவ்வளவு நேரம்?" — ln பயன்படுத்துங்கள் TNEB AE (EEE) — RC · RL · RLC (Tamil) 1921 p 1921 · ⌂ Index

Charging: t = τ · ln[V / (V − v)] | Discharging: t = τ · ln(V₀ / v) எல்லா case-க்கும் ஒரே formula: v(t) = Vfinal + (Vstart − Vfinal) · e−t/τ ① Vstart: switch-க்கு முன் capacitor-ல் இருந்த volt (திடீரென மாறாது) ② Vfinal: நீண்ட நேரம் கழித்து (DC-ல் C = open) ③ τ = Rth·C (source-களை kill செய்து பார்க்கும் R) GATE 2019 Q.41: 0.1 μF, 100 V-க்கு charge; 1 kΩ வழியாக discharge; 1 V வர நேரம்? τ = 1000 × 0.1×10⁻⁶ = 0.1 ms → t = 0.1 × ln(100/1) = 0.1 × 4.605 = 0.46 ms Trap: ln போடுங்கள், log அல்ல (log போட்டால் 0.2 ms — தவறு) · Rth பயன்படுத்துங்கள், series R மட்டும் அல்ல · 1 kΩ × 1 μF = 1 ms. TNEB AE (EEE) — RC · RL · RLC (Tamil) 1922 p 1922 · ⌂ Index

பகுதி 2 · RL — நீண்ட குழாயில் கனமான நீர் கதை Inductor = நீண்ட குழாயில் ஓடும் கனமான நீர் (வேகம் = current) பம்ப் = V நீரின் எடை (inertia) = L வால்வ் திடீரென மூடினால் ஓடும் நீர் உடனே நிற்காது → பெரிய அழுத்தம் (water hammer) = voltage spike கதை: ஒரு நீண்ட குழாயில் நிறைய நீர் இருக்கிறது. பம்பை ஆன் செய்தால் அந்த கனமான நீர் உடனே வேகம் எடுக்காது — மெதுவாக வேகம் கூடும் (current மெதுவாக ஏறும்). ஓடிக்கொண்டிருக்கும் நீரை வால்வால் திடீரென நிறுத்தினால் அது உடனே நிற்காது — 'தட்' என்று பெரிய அழுத்தம் (water hammer) வரும். Inductor-ல் இது தான் voltage spike. மின்சாரம் தண்ணீர் கதை Current i குழாயில் நீரின் வேகம் Inductance L நீரின் எடை / குழாயின் நீளம் (inertia) Resistance R உராய்வு — நீரின் இறுதி வேகத்தைத் தீர்மானிக்கும் Voltage spike Water hammer (வால்வை திடீரென மூடும்போது) Time constant τ = L / R (R பெரிது → வேகமாக!) Current ஏறுதல்: i = If(1 − e−t/τ), If = V/R 0 1 2 3 4 5 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1 t / τ பின்னம் 63.2 % i / I(final) vL / V (coil voltage) Switch ON: current மெதுவாக ஏறுகிறது; coil voltage முதலில் முழு V, பிறகு குறைகிறது Current இறங்குதல்: i = I₀ e−t/τ — ஆனால் voltage பாயும்! TNEB AE (EEE) — RC · RL · RLC (Tamil) 1923 p 1923 · ⌂ Index

உதாரணம்: L = 0.5 H, coil R = 10 Ω, V = 20 V → I = 2 A, τ (ஏறும்போது) = 0.5/10 = 50 ms. Supply-ஐ நீக்கி 40 Ω வழியாக discharge: மொத்த R = 50 Ω → τ = 10 ms (வேகம் அதிகம்). 0⁺-ல் current இன்னும் 2 A → 40 Ω-ல் voltage = 2 × 40 = 80 V (supply-ஐ விட 4 மடங்கு!). Switch-ஐ திறந்தால் (R → ∞) spike இன்னும் பெரிது → arc. 0 1 2 3 4 5 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1 t / τ பின்னம் 36.8 % i / I₀ Decay: current மெதுவாக குறைகிறது; ஆனால் 0⁺-ல் voltage திடீரென பாய்கிறது நடைமுறையில்: relay coil-க்கு freewheeling diode · alternator / DC machine field-க்கு field discharge resistor · CT secondary-ஐ ஒருபோதும் open செய்யக்கூடாது — எல்லாம் இதே காரணம். i(t) = Ifinal + (Istart − Ifinal) · e−t/τ GATE 2021 Q.29: switch-க்கு முன் iL = 10 A; பின் Ifinal = 8 A, τ = 0.5/5 = 0.1 s → i = 8 + 2e−10t A. Trap: τ = L/R (L × R அல்ல) · ஏறும்போதும் இறங்கும்போதும் R வேறு → τ வேறு · current தொடர்ச்சி; voltage அல்ல · mH ÷ Ω = ms. TNEB AE (EEE) — RC · RL · RLC (Tamil) 1924 p 1924 · ⌂ Index

பகுதி 3 · RLC — U-குழாய் ஊஞ்சல் கதை RLC = U-குழாயில் ஆடும் நீர் (ஊஞ்சல் மாதிரி) உயரம் (C-ல் சேமிப்பு) ஓடும் நீர் (L-ல் சேமிப்பு) உராய்வு = R R குறைவு → பல முறை ஆடும் R அதிகம் → ஆடாமல் மெதுவாக ஆற்றல் C ↔ L மாறி மாறி செல்லும்; R அதை வெப்பமாக்கி நிறுத்தும் கதை: U-குழாயின் ஒரு பக்கம் நீரை உயர்த்தி விட்டால், நீர் மறுபக்கம் ஓடி, மீண்டும் திரும்பி — ஊஞ்சல் மாதிரி ஆடும். உயரம் = capacitor-ல் சேமிப்பு (voltage), ஓடும் நீர் = inductor-ல் சேமிப்பு (current). உராய்வு (R) தான் ஆட்டத்தை நிறுத்துகிறது. உராய்வு குறைவு → பல முறை ஆடும் (underdamped); சரியான அளவு → ஆடாமல் வேகமாக நிலைக்கு வரும் (critical); அதிகம் → மிக மெதுவாக (overdamped). Series RLC Parallel RLC இயல் அதிர்வெண் ω₀ = 1/√(LC) Damping ratio ζ (R/2)·√(C/L) (1/2R)·√(L/C) Critical R R = 2√(L/C) R = ½√(L/C) R பெரிதானால் அதிக damping (ஆட்டம் குறையும்) குறைவான damping (ஆட்டம் கூடும்!) 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 0 0.4 0.8 1.2 1.6 ω₀ t vC / V overshoot 44.4 % ζ = 0.25 (under) ζ = 1 (critical) ζ = 2 (over) DC step-ல் capacitor voltage: underdamped ஆடுகிறது, critical வேகமாக நிலைக்கு வருகிறது, overdamped மெதுவாக TNEB AE (EEE) — RC · RL · RLC (Tamil) 1925 p 1925 · ⌂ Index

g.d: What goes up when something else goes up — the idea, then circuits, machines, power and maths.
p: DIRECT & INVERSE PROPORTION — 1. THE IDEA IN PICTURES NUMERATOR → DIRECT · DENOMINATOR → INVERSE · POWER → HOW FAST The five shapes of proportion y y y y y x x x x x Direct y ∝ x Inverse y ∝ 1/x Square y ∝ x² Inverse square y ∝ Root y ∝ √x y = kx · straight line xy = k · hyperbola parabola 1/x² rises slowly x × 2 → y × 2 x × 2 → y ÷ 2 x × 2 → y × 4 falls very fast x × 4 → y × 2 x × 2 → y ÷ 4 How to read any formula Directly proportional (y ∝ x): when x goes up, y goes up by the same factor. The ratio y/x stays constant. Example: I ∝ V for a fixed resistor. Inversely proportional (y ∝ 1/x): when x goes up, y goes down by the same factor. The product xy stays constant. Example: I ∝ 1/R for a fixed voltage. Read a formula in 5 seconds: anything in the numerator → direct; anything in the denominator → inverse. A square on top → ×4 when doubled; a square below → ÷4. A square root → ×√2 when doubled. Exam trick: write new/old = (factor)^power for each variable and multiply. E.g. P = V²/R with V × 2 and R × 2 → P × (2² / 2) = × 2. Change table — x changes, what happens to y? Relation x changes x changes x changes y ∝ x ×2 → ×2 ×3 → ×3 ÷2 → ÷2 y ∝ 1/x ×2 → ÷2 ×3 → ÷3 ÷2 → ×2 y ∝ x² ×2 → ×4 ×3 → ×9 ÷2 → ÷4 y ∝ 1/x² ×2 → ÷4 ×3 → ÷9 ÷2 → ×4 y ∝ √x ×4 → ×2 ×9 → ×3 ÷4 → ÷2 y ∝ 1/√x ×4 → ÷2 ×9 → ÷3 ÷4 → ×2 y ∝ x³ ×2 → ×8 ×3 → ×27 ÷2 → ÷8
