g.d: Element by element: what a short or an open does.
p: SHORT-CIRCUIT & OPEN-CIRCUIT — WHAT CHANGES? (1) THE GENERAL RULE · DC MACHINES · TRANSFORMERS, CT & PT The general rule SHORT circuit → resistance/impedance in that path ≈ 0 → current rises, unless the short also kills the field (shunt generator) — then everything collapses. OPEN circuit → current in that path stops. If the open part was carrying opposing ampere-turns or a winding is cut by changing flux (CT secondary, synchronous-motor field at start), a dangerous high voltage appears. Field winding rule: field opposing (differential) removed → flux ↑; field aiding (cumulative) removed → flux ↓; field lost in a motor → speed ↑↑ (N ∝ 1/φ). Tests use this on purpose: short-circuit / blocked-rotor test → copper loss and impedance; open-circuit / no-load test → iron loss and magnetising current. DC machines What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Series field shorted — DIFFERENTIAL compound generator Terminal voltage RISES (20 % / 80 % case: +33 %) Series flux was opposing → removed → net φ ↑ → E ∝ φ ↑ Series field shorted — CUMULATIVE compound generator Terminal voltage FALLS (works like a shunt generator) Series flux was aiding → removed → net φ ↓ → E ↓ Low resistance (diverter) across the series field Less compounding (over-compound → flat) Part of the load current bypasses the series field Shunt field OPEN — generator Voltage collapses to the small residual value Field current 0 → only residual flux Shunt field OPEN — motor running Speed rises dangerously, armature current very high φ → residual → N ∝ 1/φ → runaway; E b falls → I a ↑ Shunt field shorted — motor Same as field loss: over-speed / overcurrent Field winding gets no voltage → φ collapses Terminals shorted — SHUNT generator Current rises briefly, then falls to a small value V = 0 → shunt field loses excitation → E collapses (self-protecting) Terminals shorted — SEPARATELY excited or SERIES generator Very large current — damage unless tripped Field is not weakened (series field even strengthens) → I = E/R a Armature locked / starter shorted at start Huge current I = V/R a N = 0 → E b = 0 → nothing limits current except R a Series field shorted — series motor Flux ≈ 0 → very high speed and current N ∝ 1/φ with almost no flux

Transformer, CT and PT What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Secondary shorted at RATED voltage Current ≈ I rated / Z pu (5 % → 20 ×): heat and huge forces → protection trips Only the small leakage impedance limits current Secondary shorted at REDUCED voltage (SC test) Rated current flows at ~5–10 % voltage → copper loss and Z eq measured Flux is tiny at low voltage → iron loss negligible Secondary OPEN (no load / OC test) Only no-load current (2–5 %) → iron loss and magnetising branch measured No load current → copper loss negligible CT secondary OPEN while primary carries current Very high voltage at secondary + core overheats → dangerous No opposing secondary ampere-turns → all primary current magnetises the core → saturation CT secondary shorted Safe — this is the normal state (burden is a near short) Secondary ampere-turns balance the primary PT secondary shorted Very high current → PT burns (protected by fuses) PT is a voltage transformer with tiny leakage impedance Few turns shorted (inter-turn fault) Heavy local current, heating, gas → Buchholz relay operates Shorted turns act as a shorted secondary Primary connected to DC Very high current → winding burns f = 0 → no back EMF → only winding resistance

SHORT-CIRCUIT & OPEN-CIRCUIT — WHAT CHANGES? (2) INDUCTION MOTOR · SYNCHRONOUS MACHINE Induction motor What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Slip-ring rotor terminals shorted Normal running (like a squirrel cage) Rotor circuit closed → rotor current → torque Slip-ring rotor OPEN No torque — motor does not start; stator takes only magnetising current No rotor current → no torque (like an open-secondary transformer) Rotor resistance shorted step by step during start Smooth acceleration, then normal running High R at start → high T st ; removed at speed for efficiency One supply phase OPEN while running (single phasing) Keeps running, current in other lines ↑ → overheating Runs as a 1-φ motor; needs a single-phasing preventer One supply phase OPEN at standstill Does not start — only hums Single-phase field gives no starting torque Rotor blocked (blocked-rotor test) s = 1: at full V current is 5–7 ×; at reduced V gives copper loss and Z eq Like a transformer short-circuit test No-load test (rotor free, no load) Small current → iron + friction losses Like a transformer open-circuit test Synchronous machine What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Sudden 3-phase short at alternator terminals Very high first current (X″ d ), then falls (X′ d ) to steady value (X d ) Subtransient → transient → steady state as damper and field currents decay Steady short-circuit (SC test) Rated current flows at a small field current; SCC is a straight line Large X s + demagnetising armature reaction keep the core unsaturated Armature OPEN (OC test) Terminal voltage = E; gives the OCC No armature current → no reaction, no drop Field OPEN — generator on the grid (loss of excitation) Runs as an induction generator, draws large reactive power, may slip poles E collapses → excitation must come from the grid Field OPEN while starting a synchronous motor Dangerous high voltage induced in the field winding Rotating field cuts many field turns at slip frequency → field is shorted through a resistor during starting Excitation removed — synchronous motor on load Pulls out of step or runs with large lagging current E → 0 → P max = EV/X s → 0 Stationary alternator switched onto live bus-bars Acts like a SHORT CIRCUIT — very large current, heavy torque shock At standstill E = 0, so the bus voltage drives current through X s alone (TNPSC 2026 Q187) — always sy

SHORT-CIRCUIT & OPEN-CIRCUIT — WHAT CHANGES? (3) SINGLE-PHASE MOTORS · POWER SYSTEM Single-phase motors What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Starting capacitor OPEN Motor hums, does not start (runs if pushed) No phase split → no rotating field at standstill Starting capacitor shorted Auxiliary winding draws high current → overheats / fuse blows Capacitor no longer limits or shifts current Centrifugal switch fails to open Auxiliary winding overheats and burns Starting winding is designed only for short duty Centrifugal switch fails to close (stuck open) Motor does not start Auxiliary winding never connected Universal motor load removed Very high speed Series motor: N ∝ 1/I a Power system What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) 3-phase short circuit Highest fault current, voltage at the fault → 0 Only positive-sequence impedance limits current Line-to-ground fault on a solidly earthed system High fault current in the faulted phase Zero-sequence path exists through earth Line-to-ground fault on an isolated-neutral system Small fault current but healthy phases rise to line voltage (√3 ×) No return path; neutral shifts Neutral OPEN in a 4-wire system with unbalanced load Phase voltages unbalance — some go above rated → appliances damaged No path for unbalance current → star point floats Earth (body) connection OPEN Touch voltage on equipment body during a fault Fault current has no low-resistance path Current-limiting reactor shorted Fault level rises Less series impedance in the fault path

SHORT-CIRCUIT & OPEN-CIRCUIT — WHAT CHANGES? (4) CIRCUITS & TRANSIENTS · TWO-PORT Circuits & transients What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Switch closed for a long time (DC steady state) Capacitor = OPEN, inductor = SHORT dv/dt = 0 → i C = 0; di/dt = 0 → v L = 0 Switching instant t = 0⁺ Uncharged C = SHORT, current-free L = OPEN; otherwise v C and i L keep their t = 0⁻ values Capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot jump (GATE 2010 Q15, 2021 Q39) Long after switching (t → ∞, DC) C open, L short again → read the final values e −t/τ terms have died out (≈ 5τ) Load terminals OPENED Thevenin voltage V th = open-circuit voltage No load current, so no internal drop (TNPSC 2026 Q146) Load terminals SHORTED Norton current I N = short-circuit current; R th = V oc /I sc Works even with dependent sources Independent source ‘killed’ Voltage source → SHORT, current source → OPEN Used in superposition and to find R th ; dependent sources stay Nullator in series with an element Whole branch acts as OPEN (I = 0) Nullator: V = 0 and I = 0 (GATE 2025 Q19) Two-port What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Port 2 SHORTED (V₂ = 0) y₁₁ = I₁/V₁, y₂₁ = I₂/V₁, h₁₁ = V₁/I₁, h₂₁ = I₂/I₁, B = −V₁/I₂, D = −I₁/I₂ Short-circuit (y) parameters; h₁₁, h₂₁ need V₂ = 0 Port 2 OPENED (I₂ = 0) z₁₁ = V₁/I₁, z₂₁ = V₂/I₁, A = V₁/V₂, C = I₁/V₂ Open-circuit (z) parameters; A, C need I₂ = 0 Port 1 SHORTED (V₁ = 0) y₁₂ = I₁/V₂, y₂₂ = I₂/V₂ Drive port 2, short port 1 Port 1 OPENED (I₁ = 0) z₁₂ = V₁/I₂, z₂₂ = V₂/I₂, h₁₂ = V₁/V₂, h₂₂ = I₂/V₂ Drive port 2, open port 1 (AE 2018 Q62)

SHORT-CIRCUIT & OPEN-CIRCUIT — WHAT CHANGES? (5) TRANSMISSION LINE · SOLAR CELL Transmission line What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Receiving end OPEN (no load) V R rises above V S (Ferranti): V R = V S /cos βl; sending current = charging current only Line capacitance draws leading current through the series L Travelling wave reaches an OPEN end Voltage doubles, current becomes 0 Γ v = +1 (TNPSC 2025 Q32: V r = 2 × incident) Travelling wave reaches a SHORTED end Voltage becomes 0, current doubles Γ v = −1 Shunt reactor switched in at light load Receiving-end voltage falls back to normal Absorbs the line's charging VARs (GATE 2014 Q26) Solar cell What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Solar cell terminals OPEN V = V oc (≈ 0.5–0.6 V for Si), I = 0, P = 0 All photo-current flows through the diode Solar cell terminals SHORTED I = I sc (∝ irradiance), V = 0, P = 0 Fill factor FF = P max /(V oc ·I sc ); MPP lies between the two

SHORT-CIRCUIT & OPEN-CIRCUIT — WHAT CHANGES? (6) PROTECTION Protection What is shorted / opened What happens Why (cause → effect) Short circuit on a feeder with HRC fuse + circuit breaker HRC fuse clears the heavy short-circuit current; the CB trips for overloads and small faults Fuse is faster and has a huge breaking capacity (TNPSC 2025 Q16) CT secondary OPEN in service Dangerous high voltage, core saturates No opposing secondary ampere-turns — always short the CT before removing the relay

g.d: Twelve pages of “double this, halve that” — the answer and the reason.
p: WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (1) FREQUENCY · VOLTAGE · LOAD · EXCITATION — THE RULES · TRANSFORMER The rules (learn these 5 lines) Excitation current I₀ = magnetising current I m (makes the flux, lags V by 90°) + core-loss current I w (in phase). It is set by flux, not by load. Flux rule: E = 4.44 f N φ → φ ∝ V/f. f ↑ at same V → φ ↓ → I₀ ↓. f ↓ at same V → φ ↑ → saturation → I₀ ↑↑. V/f constant → φ constant. Losses: hysteresis P h ∝ f·B 1.6 ; eddy P e ∝ f²B² ∝ V² (same V → eddy SAME). Copper loss ∝ I² (load). Reactance X = 2πfL ∝ f. 50 → 60 Hz at same V: φ × 0.83 · I₀ ↓ · P h × 0.90 · P e same · X × 1.2 · speed N s × 1.2 · T max × 0.69. Load ↑ changes currents and Cu loss only; flux and iron loss stay SAME (transformer, shunt motor). Excitation on a grid changes only Q (pf), never P or f. Transformer Excitation (no-load) current I₀ = magnetising current I m (makes flux) + core-loss current I w . Core flux φ m ∝ V/f (E = 4.44 f N φ m ). Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why Frequency 50 → 60 Hz, same V (60 Hz OK for a 50 Hz design) leakage reactance X (× 1.2) → regulation ↑ flux φ m (× 0.83), excitation current I₀, hysteresis loss (× 0.90), total iron loss eddy loss (∝ V²), secondary voltage, turns ratio, Cu loss at the same load φ ∝ V/f; P h ∝ f·B¹·⁶; P e ∝ f²B² ∝ V²; X = 2πfL Frequency 60 → 50 Hz, same V (60 Hz design used on 50 Hz) flux (× 1.2) → saturation, excitation current (large), hysteresis loss, heating leakage reactance eddy loss, secondary voltage Same V at lower f needs more flux → core saturates → I₀ rises sharply Primary voltage ↑ 10 %, same f flux, excitation current I₀ (more than 10 % — saturation), iron loss (hysteresis and eddy), secondary voltage (+10 %) — turns ratio, frequency φ ∝ V; iron loss rises with flux Frequency 50 → 60 Hz with the SAME flux (sum: E₁ = 200 V → E₂ ?) induced EMF E (× 1.2: 200 → 240 V), iron losses — flux φ m , turns E = 4.44 f N φ → E ∝ f; same V instead → E same, φ × 0.83 V and f both ↑ by the same ratio (V/f constant) hysteresis loss (∝ f), eddy loss (∝ f²), kVA that can be handled — flux φ m , excitation current (approx.) V/f constant keeps flux constant Load current ↑ (same V, f) I₁ and I₂, copper loss (∝ I²), voltage drop (regulation, lagging pf) secondary terminal voltage (lagging / unity pf) mutual flux φ m , iron loss, excitation current Flux is set by V/f, not by load (I₁N₁ ≈ I₂N₂) Load

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (2) INDUCTION MOTOR Induction motor Air-gap flux φ ∝ V/f. N s = 120f/P. T ∝ V² (fixed f). T max ∝ (V/f)² and does not depend on rotor resistance. Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why Frequency 50 → 60 Hz, same V synchronous speed and running speed (× 1.2), reactances flux (× 0.83), magnetising current, T max (× 0.69), T st (≈ × 0.58 if X₂ ≫ R₂) number of poles, rotor resistance N s ∝ f; φ ∝ V/f; T max ∝ (V/f)²; T st ∝ V²/f³ (X₂ ≫ R₂) Frequency ↓, same V flux → saturation, magnetising current, heating, T max speed — φ ∝ V/f — why a VFD lowers V with f V and f changed together (V/f constant, VFD) speed (∝ f) — flux, T max (approx.), magnetising current Constant flux → constant torque capability Supply voltage ↓ 10 %, same load torque slip, rotor current, stator current, copper loss, temperature torque available (× 0.81), speed (slightly), flux, iron loss synchronous speed T ∝ sV²: lower V → more slip needed for the same torque Supply voltage ↑ 10 % torque (× 1.21), flux, magnetising current, iron loss slip (same load), pf at light load synchronous speed T ∝ V²; φ ∝ V Load torque ↑ (V, f same) slip, rotor and stator current, copper loss, pf (up to full load) speed (slightly) synchronous speed, flux, iron loss More slip → more rotor EMF and current → more torque Rotor resistance ↑ (slip-ring) starting torque (until R₂ = X₂), slip at T max , slip at the same load starting current, speed at load, efficiency T max s m = R₂/X₂; T max independent of R₂ Number of poles ↑ (same f) torque per ampere (low-speed motor) synchronous speed frequency N s = 120f/P

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (3) SYNCHRONOUS MACHINE Synchronous machine P = EV sin δ / X s . Governor/prime mover → P and f. Excitation (field current) → E, V and Q. Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why Excitation ↑ — motor on infinite bus, same load E, leading kVAR (pf goes lagging → unity → leading) load angle δ (E sin δ = constant) real power P, speed, frequency V curve: I a falls to minimum at unity pf, then rises Excitation ↑ — generator on infinite bus lagging kVAR supplied (pf more lagging) load angle δ real power P, V, f Grid fixes V and f; excitation only sets Q Excitation ↑ — stand-alone generator terminal voltage — frequency, real power No grid: E sets V directly Governor (steam/water) input ↑ — on infinite bus real power P, load angle δ — frequency, speed, terminal V Grid fixes f; more input → more P Governor input ↑ — stand-alone speed and frequency — — f = PN/120 — governor is used to hold f Load ↑ — stand-alone, no control load angle, armature current speed and frequency, terminal V (lagging load) — T elec > T mech → rotor slows; armature reaction lowers V Load ↑ — synchronous motor load angle δ, armature current — speed (= N s ), frequency Speed is fixed; only δ changes (until 90°) Supply frequency 50 → 60 Hz — motor speed (× 1.2) — number of poles N s = 120f/P Synchronous reactance X s ↑ — P max , stability margin frequency P max = EV/X s

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (4) DC MOTOR & GENERATOR DC motor & generator Motor: N ∝ (V − I a ·R a )/φ, T = kφI a . Generator: E = PφZN/(60A) ∝ φN. Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why Field current ↓ (field weakening) — motor, same load torque speed, armature current flux, torque per ampere supply voltage N ∝ 1/φ; T = kφI a needs more I a Armature voltage ↓ (separately excited field) — speed (∝ V) flux, torque capability Armature-voltage control below base speed Supply voltage ↑ — shunt motor (field on same supply) flux, field current — speed (approx., unsaturated) E b ∝ φN with φ ∝ V → N ≈ constant Load torque ↑ — shunt motor armature current, I a ·R a drop speed (slightly) flux E b = V − I a ·R a falls a little Load torque ↓ — series motor speed (dangerously) armature current, flux supply voltage N ∝ 1/I a — never run without load Extra resistance in armature circuit losses speed at load, efficiency no-load speed (approx.) More I a ·R drop → lower E b Speed ↑ — generator, same field generated EMF (∝ N) — flux E ∝ φN Field current ↑ — generator flux and EMF (until saturation) — speed Follows the OCC Speed ↓ below critical speed — shunt generator — EMF (fails to build up) field resistance Field resistance line above the OCC tangent

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (5) TRANSMISSION LINE Transmission line P max = V s ·V r /X ∝ V²/X. For the same power: I ∝ 1/V, loss ∝ 1/V², conductor volume ∝ 1/V². X ∝ length. Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why Voltage halved (800 → 400 kV), X same current for the same power (× 2), loss (× 4) P max (÷ 4 → P/4), SIL (÷ 4) X, length P max = V s ·V r /X: both V halve Voltage doubled, same power efficiency, P max (× 4), SIL (× 4), insulation cost current (÷ 2), loss (÷ 4), % voltage drop (÷ 4), conductor volume (÷ 4) power, pf I = P/(√3 V cos φ); loss = 3I²R Series capacitor added (k % compensation) P max (× 1/(1 − k)), stability, voltage at receiving end net reactance X(1 − k), load angle δ for the same P line voltage rating Cancels part of X L Second circuit in parallel (double circuit) P max (× 2), reliability X (÷ 2), load angle δ voltage Two equal reactances in parallel Line length doubled X (× 2), charging current, Ferranti rise P max (÷ 2), stability margin voltage rating X, C ∝ length Power factor improved (lagging → unity), same P efficiency, receiving voltage current, loss (∝ 1/cos²φ), voltage drop real power I = P/(√3 V cos φ) Load ↓ to light load / no load receiving-end voltage (Ferranti effect) current, loss, voltage drop sending voltage Charging current through L raises V r

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (6) POWER ELECTRONICS Power electronics Most answers come from V dc = V do cos α, V o = D·V s and ΔI = V·D(1 − D)/(f·L). Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why Gate current ↑ (and anode voltage ↑) — SCR rate of rise of anode current turn-on delay time holding & latching current stronger gate drive injects carriers faster (TNPSC 2025 Q199) Firing angle α ↑ — full converter, continuous current reactive power drawn V dc ∝ cos α, input pf (0.9 cos α) ripple frequency (2f, 6f) α > 90° → V dc negative (inverting) Duty ratio D ↑ — buck / boost V o = D·V s (buck), V s /(1 − D) (boost) — switching frequency volt-second balance on L Back EMF of a chopper-fed motor ↑ 10 %, same D — average armature current (D·V − E)/R current ripple ΔI ΔI depends on V, D, f, L — not on E (TNPSC 2026 Q39) Switching frequency f ↑ switching loss (∝ f) current & voltage ripple (∝ 1/f), size of L and C average output voltage ΔI = (V s − V o )D/(f·L) Source inductance L s ↑ overlap angle μ average output V dc (drop 3ωL s ·I d /π) firing angle α commutation takes longer Load inductance ↑ (RL load) smoothness — current becomes continuous current ripple average current for the same V dc and R L opposes change of current

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (7) CONTROL SYSTEM Control system Unity feedback G = K/[s(s + a)]: s² + as + K = 0 → ω n = √K, ζ = a/(2√K), ζω n = a/2 fixed. Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why Forward gain K ↑ ω n , overshoot M p , bandwidth, K v ζ, ramp error 1/K v , phase margin settling time 4/(ζω n ) = 8/a ζ ∝ 1/√K PI controller added type (+1), overshoot steady-state error (step → 0) — adds a pole at the origin (TNPSC 2025 Q92) PD / lead compensator added phase margin, bandwidth, speed overshoot, rise time type, steady-state error adds a zero → phase lead Lag compensator added low-frequency gain (K v ) steady-state error, bandwidth phase margin (nearly) pole near the origin: gain-limited integrator (TNPSC 2026 Q53) Negative feedback added (H ↑) bandwidth, stability margin closed-loop gain, sensitivity to G: S = 1/(1 + GH) — C/R = G/(1 + GH) Extra open-loop pole added phase lag, settling time stability margin, bandwidth — root locus bends towards the right half-plane

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (8) AMPLIFIER Amplifier Negative feedback divides or multiplies by (1 + Aβ); series mixing raises R in , voltage sampling lowers R out . Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why Feedback factor β ↑ — voltage-series (series–shunt) input impedance × (1 + Aβ), bandwidth voltage gain, output impedance ÷ (1 + Aβ), distortion gain × bandwidth GATE 2013 Q23 Temperature ↑ — BJT I CBO (doubles per 10 °C), β, I C V BE (≈ −2.5 mV/°C) — danger: thermal runaway Emitter bypass capacitor removed input resistance, bias stability, bandwidth voltage gain (≈ −R C /R E ) DC bias point unbypassed R E = series feedback Collector resistance R C ↑ — CE voltage gain |A v | = g m ·R C DC V CE , bandwidth I C (set by the base circuit) Q-point moves towards saturation

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (9) COMMUNICATION Communication PCM: SQNR = 1.76 + 6.02n dB. AM: P t = P c (1 + m²/2). FM: Carson BW = 2(Δf + f m ). Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why PCM bits n → n + 1 SQNR by 6 dB (× 4), bit rate, bandwidth step size Δ (÷ 2), noise power (÷ 4) sampling rate 5 → 7 bits: SQNR × 16 (TNPSC PG Q182) AM modulation index m ↑ (up to 1) total power, efficiency m²/(2 + m²) — carrier power, bandwidth 2f m m > 1 → over-modulation FM deviation Δf ↑ modulation index β, bandwidth, output SNR — transmitted power (constant envelope) FM power does not depend on β Sampling rate f s ↑ bit rate, bandwidth aliasing quantisation noise per sample Nyquist: f s ≥ 2f m

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (10) LOAD FLOW & STABILITY Load flow & stability Swing: M d²δ/dt² = P m − P e , M = H/(πf). Dispatch: equal incremental cost λ. Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why PV bus converted to PQ (NR, polar) unknown |V| (+1 per bus), Jacobian order (+1 per bus) — unknown voltage angles a PQ bus has both |V| and δ unknown (GATE 2016 Q29) Cost coefficient of unit 1 ↑ (economic dispatch) unit 2's share, total cost P of unit 1 total load equal incremental cost λ (GATE 2023 Q21) Inertia constant H ↑ critical clearing time rate of rise of δ, rate of frequency fall steady-state limit P max larger M → slower swing Fault cleared faster decelerating area, stability margin accelerating area, δ max pre-fault power equal-area criterion Governor droop R ↑ steady frequency drop after a load step that unit's share of the load change — Δf = −ΔP/(D + 1/R); share ∝ rating/droop

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (11) FIELDS Fields Point: E ∝ 1/r², V ∝ 1/r. Line or wire: E, H ∝ 1/r. Infinite sheet: E independent of r. Element (Biot–Savart): dH ∝ 1/R². Change (others same) Goes UP ↑ Goes DOWN ↓ Stays SAME Why Distance from a point charge doubled — E and F (× ¼), V (× ½) total charge E = Q/4πεr² Distance from a line charge / long wire doubled — E or H (× ½) — E = λ/2πεr, H = I/2πr Distance from an infinite sheet changed — — E = ρ s /2ε sheet field does not depend on distance Biot–Savart element: distance R doubled — dH (× ¼) — dH = I dl sin θ/4πR² (TNPSC 2026 Q103) Plate gap d doubled, V same — C (÷ 2), E (÷ 2), stored energy (÷ 2) V C = εA/d Dielectric εᵣ ↑, V same C, charge, stored energy — E = V/d part-filled: layers in series, sectors side by side in parallel (GATE 2019 Q30)

WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES? (12) MEASUREMENTS Measurements Shunt R sh = R m /(m − 1); multiplier R se = R m (m − 1); bridge output ∝ excitation.
